papers.title: Vaccination rates, facilitators and barriers for influenza, pneumococcal and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination among sepsis survivors: a Mid-German Sepsis Cohort survey
papers.abstract: Abstract Sepsis survivors often suffer from chronic immune dysfunction, leading to frequent rehospitalization and recurrent sepsis. Vaccinations are effective in preventing common infections in sepsis survivors. However, vaccination behavior in this vulnerable population remains unknown. Prospective interviewer-administered survey performed between 04/2023 and 04/2024 among sepsis survivors in Germany. Participants were recruited from the Mid-German Sepsis Cohort (MSC) 6 to 8 years after initial inclusion. We assessed risk perception, cues to action and barriers for vaccination against influenza, pneumococci and SARS-CoV-2. Predictors for the vaccination status of each of the three infections were identified by logistic regression analyses. Among 174 survivors, vaccination rates against influenza and pneumococci rose from 57.3 to 70.7% and from 31.4 to 60.5% 3 months to 8 years post-sepsis, respectively. A total of 135 patients (77.6%) had full vaccination coverage against SARS-CoV-2 at the time of the survey. Higher age and an intermediate vs. low education increased the odds for influenza vaccination. No associations between sociodemographic indicators and the vaccination status against pneumococci and SARS-CoV-2 were found. Vaccination counselling by a general practitioner increased the odds for vaccination between 5.5-fold (influenza) and 3.2-fold (pneumococci) in the multiple regression analyses. The review of general vaccination status was associated with a 4.7-fold increase of influenza vaccination rates and 3.1-fold increase of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rates. Among patients with at least one missing vaccination (n = 92), impaired mobility (16.8%), long waiting times in the practice (14.8%) and fear of infection in the practice (14.7%) were the most relevant barriers. There are considerable vaccination gaps in sepsis survivors. Pro-active vaccination counselling and checks of vaccination status by general practitioners may offer a great potential to increase vaccination rates and thus should be considered as an important element of sepsis aftercare.

Vaccinations are effective in preventing common infections in sepsis survivors. However, vaccination behavior in this vulnerable population remains unknown. Prospective interviewer-administered survey performed between 04/2023 and 04/2024 among sepsis survivors in Germany. Participants were recruited from the Mid-German Sepsis Cohort (MSC) 6 to 8 years after initial inclusion. We assessed risk perception, cues to action and barriers for vaccination against influenza, pneumococci and SARS-CoV-2. Predictors for the vaccination status of each of the three infections were identified by logistic regression analyses. Among 174 survivors, vaccination rates against influenza and pneumococci rose from 57.3 to 70.7% and from 31.4 to 60.5% 3 months to 8 years post-sepsis, respectively. A total of 135 patients (77.6%) had full vaccination coverage against SARS-CoV-2 at the time of the survey. Higher age and an intermediate vs. low education increased the odds for influenza vaccination. No associations between sociodemographic indicators and the vaccination status against pneumococci and SARS-CoV-2 were found. Vaccination counselling by a general practitioner increased the odds for vaccination between 5.5-fold (influenza) and 3.2-fold (pneumococci) in the multiple regression analyses. The review of general vaccination status was associated with a 4.7-fold increase of influenza vaccination rates and 3.1-fold increase of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rates. Among patients with at least one missing vaccination (n = 92), impaired mobility (16.8%), long waiting times in the practice (14.8%) and fear of infection in the practice (14.7%) were the most relevant barriers. There are considerable vaccination gaps in sepsis survivors. Pro-active vaccination counselling and checks of vaccination status by general practitioners may offer a great potential to increase vaccination rates and thus should be considered as an important element of sepsis aftercare.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores vaccination rates, facilitators, and barriers for influenza, pneumococcal, and SARS-CoV-2 vaccines among sepsis survivors in Germany. A prospective survey of 174 sepsis survivors, conducted between 2023 and 2024, revealed that vaccination rates for influenza and pneumococci increased over time, with 77.6% of participants having full SARS-CoV-2 vaccination coverage. Logistic regression analyses identified higher age and intermediate education as predictors for influenza vaccination, while general practitioner counseling significantly increased vaccination odds. Barriers such as impaired mobility, long waiting times, and fear of infection were reported among those with incomplete vaccination. The study highlights the need for proactive vaccination counseling and status checks in sepsis aftercare to address existing gaps.

papers.title: Mitigation of imprinted antibody responses against COVID-19 in highly vaccinated older adults.
papers.abstract: Despite higher clinical risk of severe COVID-19, contemporary data on antibody durability and breadth in older adults receiving multiple COVID-19 booster vaccines remain limited amid ongoing evolution of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron JN.1 descendants and the divergent BA.3.2 saltation variant. We studied a clinically vulnerable cohort of 43 older adults (median age = 85 years, IQR 75-88, 40% female). Using pseudotyped and surrogate virus neutralization-based assays, we demonstrate that JN.1 and KP.2 vaccinations six months apart elicit high-potency neutralization across all studied JN.1-lineage variants but not BA.3.2.2, where titers were 2-3-fold lower. Waning of serum neutralizing activity was modest between vaccine doses, suggesting sustained immunity. Importantly, the half-life of serum neutralization against Wu-1 (179 days) was substantially longer than JN.1 subvariants (43.7-70.1 days), consistent with Wu-1-specific imprinted responses. Furthermore, BA.3.2.2 neutralizing antibody half-life was prolonged at 107 days, implicating imprinted ancestral variant-targeting antibodies having some activity against BA.3.2.2. While absolute neutralization titers remained highest against ancestral Wu-1 due to multiple historical exposures, recall responses after the KP.2 vaccine revealed a shift in immunodominance. Neutralization against full-length Wu-1 spike was not boosted, whereas all JN.1 descendants and BA.3.2.2 showed significant boosts, indicating partial alleviation of immune imprinting. These data indicate that in the elderly, protective neutralizing antibody responses against recent variants of concern can be achieved, with reduction of immune imprinting and waning through biannual, strain-updated booster vaccines. Imprinted antibodies against ancestral variants may still be relevant for protection against highly immune evasive variants such as BA.3.2.2, highlighting that careful characterization of population-level COVID-19 humoral immunity remains warranted.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates antibody responses in older adults who received multiple booster vaccines against SARS-CoV-2, focusing on the durability and breadth of immunity against recent variants. The research highlights that despite the clinical vulnerability of this population, biannual, strain-updated booster vaccines can reduce immune imprinting and sustain neutralizing activity against emerging variants. The findings suggest that while ancestral variant-specific antibodies may persist, they do not fully impede responses to newer variants like BA.3.2.2. These results have implications for vaccine strategies in the elderly, emphasizing the need for updated formulations to maintain effective protection. However, the study's abstract-only nature and limited scope may restrict the depth of conclusions that can be drawn.

papers.title_zh: Mitigation of imprinted antibody responses against COVID-19 in highly vaccinated older adults.
papers.source_body_en: Despite higher clinical risk of severe COVID-19, contemporary data on antibody durability and breadth in older adults receiving multiple COVID-19 booster vaccines remain limited amid ongoing evolution of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron JN.1 descendants and the divergent BA.3.2 saltation variant. We studied a clinically vulnerable cohort of 43 older adults (median age = 85 years, IQR 75-88, 40% female). Using pseudotyped and surrogate virus neutralization-based assays, we demonstrate that JN.1 and KP.2 vaccinations six months apart elicit high-potency neutralization across all studied JN.1-lineage variants but not BA.3.2.2, where titers were 2-3-fold lower. Waning of serum neutralizing activity was modest between vaccine doses, suggesting sustained immunity. Importantly, the half-life of serum neutralization against Wu-1 (179 days) was substantially longer than JN.1 subvariants (43.7-70.1 days), consistent with Wu-1-specific imprinted responses. Furthermore, BA.3.2.2 neutralizing antibody half-life was prolonged at 107 days, implicating imprinted ancestral variant-targeting antibodies having some activity against BA.3.2.2. While absolute neutralization titers remained highest against ancestral Wu-1 due to multiple historical exposures, recall responses after the KP.2 vaccine revealed a shift in immunodominance. Neutralization against full-length Wu-1 spike was not boosted, whereas all JN.1 descendants and BA.3.2.2 showed significant boosts, indicating partial alleviation of immune imprinting. These data indicate that in the elderly, protective neutralizing antibody responses against recent variants of concern can be achieved, with reduction of immune imprinting and waning through biannual, strain-updated booster vaccines. Imprinted antibodies against ancestral variants may still be relevant for protection against highly immune evasive variants such as BA.3.2.2, highlighting that careful characterization of population-level COVID-19 humoral immunity remains warranted.

papers.title: Associations between salivary HHV-6 and long COVID severity in a cross-sectional, case-control analysis.
papers.abstract: Background Reactivation of human herpesviruses (HHVs), particularly EBV, is associated with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of Long COVID (LC). Reactivation of HHVs has been previously implicated in hormonal dysregulation, which has also been observed in LC, suggesting a potential link. This study aims to examine the relationship between LC symptoms and salivary HHV DNA, cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol levels. Methods Our cross-sectional, case-control study enrolled 45 participants with LC, and 45 age-sex-matched controls. Surveys and validated health questionnaires were used to collect demographics, medical history, and symptom profiles. Saliva was self-collected at waking, 15, 30, and 45 min, and 8 and 16 h after waking, across two consecutive days. Salivary cortisol, testosterone and oestradiol were measured, and extracted nucleic acid was tested for EBV, HSV 1/2, HCMV and HHV-6 A/B using multiplex qPCR, and for SARS-CoV-2 and RNaseP using RT-qPCR. Findings Detection of salivary EBV and HHV-6 DNA copies was highest early in the morning. There were no significant differences in salivary cortisol, testosterone, or oestradiol, or in EBV or HHV-6 DNA between the LC and control groups. However, salivary HHV-6 DNA levels were positively associated with a greater aggregated LC propensity score (r = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.02-0.44, p = 0.015, adj. p = 0.030), as well as anxiety (β = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.02-1.36, p = 0.045) and depression (β = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.05-0.42, p = 0.013) scores. Interpretation The observed correlation between salivary HHV-6 DNA and symptom severity suggests HHV-6 may contribute to post-acute disease, though mechanisms remain unclear. While we did not identify a relationship between salivary EBV DNA and LC, EBV may still play a role at earlier time points in the disease course, or in compartments not sampled in this study. These findings highlight the potential importance of HHV-6 in LC pathophysiology and underscore the need for longitudinal, multi-compartment studies of herpesvirus reactivation in LC. Funding This work was supported in part by the Else Kröner Fresenius Prize for Medical Research 2023 (to AI), the Howard Hughes Medical Institute Collaborative COVID-19 Initiative (to AI), and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (to AI), the Polybio Research Foundation (to AI and DP) and the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation (to DP). National Institutes for Health (NIH) funding sources supported AT, SB and CM.

papers.abstract_original: Background Reactivation of human herpesviruses (HHVs), particularly EBV, is associated with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of Long COVID (LC). Reactivation of HHVs has been previously implicated in hormonal dysregulation, which has also been observed in LC, suggesting a potential link. This study aims to examine the relationship between LC symptoms and salivary HHV DNA, cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol levels. Methods Our cross-sectional, case-control study enrolled 45 participants with LC, and 45 age-sex-matched controls. Surveys and validated health questionnaires were used to collect demographics, medical history, and symptom profiles. Saliva was self-collected at waking, 15, 30, and 45 min, and 8 and 16 h after waking, across two consecutive days. Salivary cortisol, testosterone and oestradiol were measured, and extracted nucleic acid was tested for EBV, HSV 1/2, HCMV and HHV-6 A/B using multiplex qPCR, and for SARS-CoV-2 and RNaseP using RT-qPCR. papers.title: Association Between Acute Vulvar Ulcers and Gene-Based COVID-19 Vaccines.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Acute vulvar ulcers have been reported following gene-based COVID-19 vaccinations, though causality remains uncertain. This study aims to examine the association between vaccination and ulcer occurrence. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This observational study analyzed vulvar ulcer cases reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) from January 2002 to February 2022. Risk was estimated by comparing VAERS-reported ulcer cases with vaccine recipient data from the COVID Data Tracker. Causality was assessed using the Bradford Hill criteria. RESULTS: From 2021 to 2022, the proportion of vulvar ulcers among reported adverse events exceeded the upper control limits for the first time since 2002. Most cases (134/137, 97.8%) were linked to COVID-19 vaccines. Ad26.COV2.S had the highest relative risk (2.72 vs. BNT162b2; 95% CI: 1.17-6.30). For two-dose vaccines, the second dose posed a higher risk (dose 2 vs. dose 1: RR 3.52; 95% CI: 2.06-6.02 for BNT162b2; RR 2.40; 95% CI: 1.82-3.18 for mRNA-1273). Ulcers appeared a median of 2 days post-vaccination (IQR: 1.25-2.75) and resolved after a median of 12 days (IQR: 7-18). Adolescent females aged 12-17 years had the highest risk (RR vs. age 25-39: 4.01; 95% CI: 2.67-6.05), with a 46.0-fold increased risk (95% CI: 11.2-188.9) compared to age-matched females who received HPV vaccines. CONCLUSIONS: Vulvar ulcers were closely associated with COVID-19 vaccination, especially in adolescent females. While findings suggest a potential link, further research is warranted to determine causality.

papers.title: Time to resolution of Long COVID symptoms and the associated factors among the people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the 3rd wave of COVID-19 in Zambia: A prospective quantitative study
papers.abstract: This study was conducted over 24 months (September 2021-Agust, 2023) to determine the time to resolution of Long COVID symptoms and the associated factors among people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the 3rd wave (June - August, 2021) of COVID-19 in Zambia. Participants comprised a cohort of 303 people randomly sampled from 7 healthcare facilities from Lusaka and Southern provinces. Demographic and clinical data were collected at baseline and at a monthly interval from participants’ clinical records and interview. Descriptive analysis was conducted to summarise respondent demographic and clinical characteristics. Survival analysis (Kaplan Meier model) was conducted to determine the median time to symptom resolution, generate survival curves and the risk table. A Poisson model was fitted to compute the crude incident rate of recovery. Cox-Proportional Hazards regression analysis was conducted to determine the univariate and multivariate association between the covariates and the time to resolution of symptoms. Crude and adjusted hazard ratios, 95% confidence intervals and p-values were computed. A total of 236 events occurred during the follow- up period; the crude incidence rate was 1, 575.6 events per 1000 person years (95%CI: 1,363.2 - 1,784.4). The median time from diagnosis of Long COVID symptoms to resolution was 6 (IQR: 5-8) months. Vaccination status was significantly associated with the time to resolution of symptoms (aHR= 1.71, 95% CI: 1.02 - 2.86, p=0.04) after adjusting for age, number of children, occupation, pre-existing medical conditions, number of vaccine doses and hospital admission. Other variables did not show statistically significant association with the time to resolution of symptoms (p>0.05). These findings suggest that vaccination is associated with a shorter time to resolution of Long COVID symptoms. Netherless, causation can not be ascertained due to the observational design of the study. A study with an experimental design is needed to establish the causal relationship.

papers.title: Pregnancy and iron deficiency anemia are associated with COVID-19 severity: a retrospective cohort study from Gaza.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: COVID-19 poses significant risks to pregnant women, with pregnancy recognized as a risk factor for severe disease. This vulnerability may be exacerbated by iron deficiency anemia (IDA) due to impaired immune function, reduced oxygen transport, and altered coagulation and endothelial function. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of 271 unvaccinated, otherwise healthy women aged 18-38 with COVID-19 was conducted at Al-Shifa Hospital, Gaza (2021). Pregnant (n = 97) and nonpregnant (n = 174) groups were stratified by IDA, investigating the impact of pregnancy and IDA on the severity of COVID-19. Iron deficiency was determined by transferrin saturation levels <20% measured during acute infection, whereas ferritin levels were not available. RESULTS: Overall pregnancy was significantly associated with COVID-19 severity (p < 0.001), with pregnant women having higher odds of critical illness (OR = 4.61, 95% CI 2.27-9.39, p < 0.001) and death (OR = 5.25, 95% CI 1.91-14.44, p = 0.001) compared with moderate illness. All deaths were due to acute respiratory distress syndrome; no venous thromboembolism cases occurred. IDA was associated with COVID-19 severity in both pregnant (p = 0.015) and non-pregnant (p = 0.002) women. In a multivariable model including pregnancy, IDA was associated with higher odds of severe (OR = 3.57, 95% CI 1.97-6.48, p < 0.001), critical (OR = 2.25, 95% CI 1.09-4.64, p = 0.029), and fatal illness (OR = 7.23, 95% CI 1.96-26.74, p = 0.003) compared with moderate illness. CONCLUSION: This study suggests that among young, otherwise healthy, unvaccinated women with COVID-19, pregnancy and IDA are associated with increased COVID-19 severity. However, interpretation requires caution considering the small number of events, particularly deaths, and the assessment of iron status during acute infection using transferrin saturation alone without ferritin measurements, which limits the ability to distinguish preexisting iron deficiency from inflammation-related changes in iron metabolism.

The authors suggest that these factors may influence disease outcomes, emphasizing the need for targeted surveillance and management. However, the study's small sample size and reliance on transferrin saturation alone to assess iron status limit the strength of the evidence, necessitating caution in interpretation.

papers.title_zh: Pregnancy and iron deficiency anemia are associated with COVID-19 severity: a retrospective cohort study from Gaza.
papers.source_body_en: INTRODUCTION: COVID-19 poses significant risks to pregnant women, with pregnancy recognized as a risk factor for severe disease. This vulnerability may be exacerbated by iron deficiency anemia (IDA) due to impaired immune function, reduced oxygen transport, and altered coagulation and endothelial function. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of 271 unvaccinated, otherwise healthy women aged 18-38 with COVID-19 was conducted at Al-Shifa Hospital, Gaza (2021). Pregnant (n = 97) and nonpregnant (n = 174) groups were stratified by IDA, investigating the impact of pregnancy and IDA on the severity of COVID-19. Iron deficiency was determined by transferrin saturation levels <20% measured during acute infection, whereas ferritin levels were not available. RESULTS: Overall pregnancy was significantly associated with COVID-19 severity (p < 0.001), with pregnant women having higher odds of critical illness (OR = 4.61, 95% CI 2.27-9.39, p < 0.001) and death (OR = 5.25, 95% CI 1.91-14.44, p = 0.001) compared with moderate illness. All deaths were due to acute respiratory distress syndrome; no venous thromboembolism cases occurred. IDA was associated with COVID-19 severity in both pregnant (p = 0.015) and non-pregnant (p = 0.002) women. In a multivariable model including pregnancy, IDA was associated with higher odds of severe (OR = 3.57, 95% CI 1.97-6.48, p < 0.001), critical (OR = 2.25, 95% CI 1.09-4.64, p = 0.029), and fatal illness (OR = 7.23, 95% CI 1.96-26.74, p = 0.003) compared with moderate illness. CONCLUSION: This study suggests that among young, otherwise healthy, unvaccinated women with COVID-19, pregnancy and IDA are associated with increased COVID-19 severity. However, interpretation requires caution considering the small number of events, particularly deaths, and the assessment of iron status during acute infection using transferrin saturation alone without ferritin measurements, which limits the ability to distinguish preexisting iron deficiency from inflammation-related changes in iron metabolism.

papers.title: Integrating Individual-Level Syndromic Surveillance Data Into Infectious Disease Modeling for COVID-19 Forecasting in Sweden: Comparative Modeling Study.
papers.abstract: Background The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered major global challenges, highlighting the need for timely surveillance and accurate forecasting to curb disease transmission and reduce the health burden. Traditional modeling approaches usually rely on aggregated data on confirmed cases. However, testing data can be unreliable due to low availability and uptake, as well as registration delays. In Sweden, the 1177 health care helpline provides valuable syndromic surveillance data that can capture early signals of infection prior to confirmation through testing. Objective This study aims to evaluate the effect of integrating syndromic surveillance data on short-term COVID-19 forecast accuracy. Methods We developed a novel epidemiological model named SI s I c HRD (susceptible-infected suspected -infected confirmed -hospitalized-recovered-deceased), incorporating data from the 1177 health care helpline cross-linked with national registers on COVID-19 testing, hospitalizations, and deaths. In the novel model, the population with infection is divided into suspected infections (I s ; those reporting symptoms to 1177) and confirmed infections (I c ; those who tested positive). Accuracy metrics of this model are compared to a model without data from the 1177 health care helpline. To evaluate model performance across different pandemic phases between March 2 and December 31, 2020, we used a daily rolling-window approach with a 60-day fitting period to predict confirmed infections, hospitalizations, and deaths over the subsequent 30 days. Prediction performance was evaluated using mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). Results The proposed SI s I c HRD model successfully captured the temporal dynamics of confirmed, hospitalized, and death cases. The model achieved a median mean MAPE of 61.6% (IQR 37.6%-79.6%) for confirmed cases, 37.5% (IQR 18.9%-57.5%) for hospitalizations and for deaths, the model achieved a median MAPE of 0.65% (IQR 0.3%-1.9%), indicating substantially higher predictive accuracy for severe outcomes compared to confirmed infections and hospital admissions. Compared to the model without syndromic surveillance data, short-term forecasting performance of the SI s I c HRD model reduced MAPE by an average of 15.7 percentage points for confirmed cases, 8.17 percentage points for hospitalizations, and 1.99 percentage points for deaths. Overall, the results demonstrate predictive stability for severe outcomes during the early phase of the pandemic. Conclusions The proposed model demonstrated predictive performance by integrating individual-level data with health care helpline syndromic data on testing and severe disease outcomes, capturing early signals from symptomatic individuals and distinguishing suspected cases from subsequently confirmed infections, leading to better forecasts of severe outcomes such as hospitalizations and deaths. This framework can support public health decision-making in future outbreaks.

papers.title_zh: Integrating Individual-Level Syndromic Surveillance Data Into Infectious Disease Modeling for COVID-19 Forecasting in Sweden: Comparative Modeling Study.
papers.source_body_en: Background The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered major global challenges, highlighting the need for timely surveillance and accurate forecasting to curb disease transmission and reduce the health burden. Traditional modeling approaches usually rely on aggregated data on confirmed cases. However, testing data can be unreliable due to low availability and uptake, as well as registration delays. In Sweden, the 1177 health care helpline provides valuable syndromic surveillance data that can capture early signals of infection prior to confirmation through testing. Objective This study aims to evaluate the effect of integrating syndromic surveillance data on short-term COVID-19 forecast accuracy. Methods We developed a novel epidemiological model named SI s I c HRD (susceptible-infected suspected -infected confirmed -hospitalized-recovered-deceased), incorporating data from the 1177 health care helpline cross-linked with national registers on COVID-19 testing, hospitalizations, and deaths. In the novel model, the population with infection is divided into suspected infections (I s ; those reporting symptoms to 1177) and confirmed infections (I c ; those who tested positive). Accuracy metrics of this model are compared to a model without data from the 1177 health care helpline. To evaluate model performance across different pandemic phases between March 2 and December 31, 2020, we used a daily rolling-window approach with a 60-day fitting period to predict confirmed infections, hospitalizations, and deaths over the subsequent 30 days. Prediction performance was evaluated using mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). Results The proposed SI s I c HRD model successfully captured the temporal dynamics of confirmed, hospitalized, and death cases. The model achieved a median mean MAPE of 61.6% (IQR 37.6%-79.6%) for confirmed cases, 37.5% (IQR 18.9%-57.5%) for hospitalizations and for deaths, the model achieved a median MAPE of 0.65% (IQR 0.3%-1.9%), indicating substantially higher predictive accuracy for severe outcomes compared to confirmed infections and hospital admissions. Compared to the model without syndromic surveillance data, short-term forecasting performance of the SI s I c HRD model reduced MAPE by an average of 15.7 percentage points for confirmed cases, 8.17 percentage points for hospitalizations, and 1.99 percentage points for deaths. Overall, the results demonstrate predictive stability for severe outcomes during the early phase of the pandemic. Conclusions The proposed model demonstrated predictive performance by integrating individual-level data with health care helpline syndromic data on testing and severe disease outcomes, capturing early signals from symptomatic individuals and distinguishing suspected cases from subsequently confirmed infections, leading to better forecasts of severe outcomes such as hospitalizations and deaths. This framework can support public health decision-making in future outbreaks.

papers.title: Coronavirus health beliefs and fetal health concerns: associations with preventive health behaviors during COVID-19.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: During infectious disease outbreaks, pregnant women and their fetuses may be especially vulnerable to health risks, emphasizing the importance of preventive health behaviors (PHB). The role of concerns about fetal health in shaping PHB during COVID-19 has never been examined. The present study examined the joint effect of concerns about fetal health and Coronavirus-related health beliefs (within the Health Belief Model) on PHB during COVID-19. METHODS: During the COVID-19 pandemic (September-November 2021), 202 pregnant Israeli women completed online questionnaires that assessed concerns about fetal health, health beliefs (perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, and barriers), and adherence to preventive health behaviors. Multiple hierarchical regression and mediation analyses were conducted. RESULTS: Concerns about fetal health were positively associated with PHB. Perceived susceptibility and perceived benefits were also positively associated with PHB, whereas perceived barriers were negatively associated; perceived severity was not significant. Mediation analyses indicated that concerns about fetal health fully mediated the association between perceived susceptibility and PHB and partially mediated the associations between perceived severity and perceived benefits and PHB. CONCLUSIONS: Concerns about fetal health play important direct and indirect roles in adhering to PHB during pregnancy. These findings may guide health services in developing tailored programs during pandemics.
papers.journal: Journal of Psychosomatic Obstetrics and Gynaecology

news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-29-october-2026-week-44 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. This report is based on data up to and including week 43 of 2026 (19 October and 25 October 2026). The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity was stable across most indicators and is circulating at low levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) increased and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents increased compared with the previous week. Weekly influenza vaccine uptake for the 2026 to 2027 season is reported for the fourth time this season. Data is for week 43 (up to 25 October 2026). Influenza vaccination data was unavailable or incomplete at the time of analysis in weeks 41 and 42, and led to several cohorts not being published in week 42. This has been corrected for this week’s report (week 43), and all cohorts are included. This will be corrected retrospectively in the report for week 42. There remains an issue that affects the attribution of vaccinations by provider setting. This is not expected to affect overall vaccination uptake estimates, which are considered to remain an accurate reflection of the influenza vaccination programme. Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 43 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (53.6% vs 56.9%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (24.8% vs 26.2%), those aged 2 years (29.7% vs 30.8%), and those aged 3 years (29.5% vs 30.7%). Vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (29.1% vs 27.8%). COVID-19 activity decreased and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness decreased. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 43 2026, 42.5% of all people aged 75 years and over in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose. Similarly, 18.2% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis were stable and below seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. As of 27 October 2026, there were a total of 1,847 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 43, decreasing from 2,151 cases in the previous week. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) PCR positivity in hospital settings decreased slightly in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 8.3% up to Sunday 25 October 2026 compared with 8.8% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.1% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This has decreased compared to 13.0% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Note 2: data from previous seasons is aligned by day. Note 3: testing policy and practice may change over time which can impact positivity rates, therefore comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. Notable changes in testing policy occurred during 2022 to 2023, which are outlined in the data quality report . Note 4: the highlighted line corresponds to the age group in the subplot title, grey lines correspond to all other age groups. Influenza positivity remained stable in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 6.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This is compared with 6.4% on the previous Sunday. By type, influenza A positivity increased slightly in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 5.8% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. Influenza B positivity increased in the same week, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 0.3% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. Influenza A positivity rates were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 16.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This has increased from 11.3% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Influenza B positivity rates for the same period were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.8%. This has decreased from 2.3% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. RSV swab-positivity based PCR test results reported through SGSS have been included as a pilot indicator from week 49 2025 onwards. RSV positivity increased in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026, compared with 1.1% up to the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 10.1% up to Sunday 25 October 2026 in week 43. This has increased from 7.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 43, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 43, 4,070 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 258 positive samples for influenza: 179 influenza A (not subtyped), 11 influenza A (H3N2), 51 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 19 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity increased slightly to 6.3% in week 43 compared with 5.9% in the previous week. In week 43, 4,952 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 376 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable at 7.6% compared with 7.3% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged between 65 and 79 years at 10.0%. RSV positivity increased to 1.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 8.3%. Adenovirus positivity increased to 1.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 5.1%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity decreased to 0.1%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 15 and 44 years at 0.4%. Parainfluenza positivity decreased slightly to 2.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 11.3%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased slightly to 16.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 29.1%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. This section is updated fortnightly. Data below was last updated in the week 43 report. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 14 September 2026 and 27 September 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the WHO influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell- and egg-based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. The characterisation of circulating A(H3N2) viruses shows that A(H3N2) viruses are currently showing low genetic diversity. All sequenced viruses to date belong to genetic subclade K. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 43 2026 (week ending 25 October 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 297 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 184 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 86 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 27 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has confirmed by genome sequencing the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in 11 influenza A/B positive samples, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared with reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. A(H1N1)pdm09: 5 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have been antigenically characterised and 3 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H1N1)pdm09 vaccine strains. A(H3N2): 6 A(H3N2) viruses have been antigenically characterised and 6 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like and A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2) like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H3N2) vaccine strains. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in table 4. There have been five detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility/resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 112 new ARI incidents reported in week 43 in England. These included: 101 incidents from care homes, of which 24 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 17 were due to influenza A, 4 were due to other pathogens, 3 were due to influenza (no type information available) and 3 were due to multiple pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 50 incidents 4 incidents from hospitals, of which 3 were due to influenza A and 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 4 incidents from educational settings, of which 2 were due to influenza (no type information available) and 1 was due to other pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 1 incident 1 incident from prisons, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 2 incidents from other settings, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available) Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 25 October 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections increased and were similar to seasonally expected levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness decreased. ED attendances for influenza-like illness increased and were above seasonally expected levels. ED attendance for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) remained stable and below seasonally expected levels. Daily NHS 111 acute respiratory infection triaged calls remained stable. GP in-hours consultation rates for COVID-19 like consultations decreased, and other respiratory infection indicators remained stable. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for acute bronchitis/bronchiolitis increased but remained below seasonally expected levels overall. Note 6: 7-day moving average is adjusted for bank holidays. Grey columns show weekends and bank holidays. Note 7: the coloured line is the 7-day moving average by age group. Grey lines show the other age groups. The y-axis shows daily attendances. It is adjusted for bank holidays. Primary care surveillance is undertaken in collaboration with the Royal College of General Practitioners ( RCGP ) Research and Surveillance Centre ( RSC ), using a national sentinel surveillance system of around 2,000 GP practices covering over 20 million registered patients of all ages across England. More information on the methodology can be found in the data quality report . The weekly ILI consultation rate through the RCGP surveillance remained stable at 6.5 per 100,000 registered population in participating GP practices in week 43. This rate is in the baseline activity level (Figure 20). By age group, the highest rates were seen in those aged under 1 year (8.3 per 100,000), and those aged between 1 and 4 years (7.4 per 100,000). The lower respiratory tract infections ( LRTI ) consultation rate remained stable at 81.6 per 100,000 in week 43 compared with 81.9 per 100,000 in the previous week. Further details are available in the weekly RSC communicable and respiratory disease report for England . MEM thresholds are based on data from the 2018 to 2019 season to the 2025 to 2026 season. Note the 2019 to 2020, 2020 to 2021 and 2021 to 2022 seasons have been removed. From week 40 2025, the RCGP sentinel swabbing scheme testing capability has been expanded to the UKHSA Bristol laboratory in addition to the UKHSA Colindale laboratory. Samples sent to Colindale are tested for influenza A and B, RSV A and B, SARS-CoV-2, hMPV , adenovirus, seasonal coronavirus and enterovirus/rhinovirus while samples sent to Bristol are tested for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS-CoV-2. 653 samples were taken in week 43 20…

Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 43 2026 (week ending 25 October 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 297 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 184 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 86 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 27 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has confirmed by genome sequencing the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in 11 influenza A/B positive samples, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared with reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. A(H1N1)pdm09: 5 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have been antigenically characterised and 3 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H1N1)pdm09 vaccine strains. A(H3N2): 6 A(H3N2) viruses have been antigenically characterised and 6 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like and A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2) like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H3N2) vaccine strains. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in table 4. There have been five detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility/resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 112 new ARI incidents reported in week 43 in England. These included: 101 incidents from care homes, of which 24 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 17 were due to influenza A, 4 were due to other pathogens, 3 were due to influenza (no type information available) and 3 were due to multiple pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 50 incidents 4 incidents from hospitals, of which 3 were due to influenza A and 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 4 incidents from educational settings, of which 2 were due to influenza (no type information available) and 1 was due to other pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 1 incident 1 incident from prisons, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 2 incidents from other settings, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available) Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 25 October 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections increased and were similar to seasonally expected levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness decreased. ED attendances for influenza-like illness increased and were above seasonally expected levels. ED attendance for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) remained stable and below seasonally expected levels. Daily NHS 111 acute respiratory infection triaged calls remained stable. GP in-hours consultation rates for COVID-19 like consultations decreased, and other respiratory infection indicators remained stable. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for acute bronchitis/bronchiolitis increased but remained below seasonally expected levels overall. Note 6: 7-day moving average is adjusted for bank holidays. Grey columns show weekends and bank holidays. Note 7: the coloured line is the 7-day moving average by age group. Grey lines show the other age groups. The y-axis shows daily attendances. It is adjusted for bank holidays. Primary care surveillance is undertaken in collaboration with the Royal College of General Practitioners ( RCGP ) Research and Surveillance Centre ( RSC ), using a national sentinel surveillance system of around 2,000 GP practices covering over 20 million registered patients of all ages across England. More information on the methodology can be found in the data quality report . The weekly ILI consultation rate through the RCGP surveillance remained stable at 6.5 per 100,000 registered population in participating GP practices in week 43. analysis.time: The report was published on 29 October 2026 (week 44), and the data is based on information up to and including week 43 of 2026 (19 October and 25 October 2026).
analysis.location_and_population: The report covers England, focusing on the population aged 75 years and over, as well as those under 75 years with a weakened immune system.
analysis.event: The report details the surveillance findings for SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), influenza, and RSV in England during week 43 of 2026. It includes data on ED attendances, confirmed ARI incidents, and influenza vaccine uptake.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of 27 October 2026, there were 1,847 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 43, a decrease from 2,151 cases in the previous week. The SARS-CoV-2 PCR positivity rate in hospital settings decreased slightly to 8.3% compared with 8.8% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.1%, down from 13.0% in the same age group the previous week.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report is based on data up to week 43 and includes information on the unified sample dataset (USD) for SARS-CoV-2 test results. It notes that testing policy and practice may change over time, which can impact positivity rates, and that comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. The data quality report outlines notable changes in testing policy during 2022 to 2023.

analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 29 October 2026 (week 44) provides an overview of the health situation in England. The report highlights that as of 27 October 2026, there were 1,847 confirmed COVID-19 cases in hospital settings during week 43, a decrease from 2,151 in the previous week. The SARS-CoV-2 PCR positivity rate in hospital settings dropped slightly to 8.3% compared with 8.8% the previous week. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over, with a rolling 7-day rate of 11.1%, down from 13.0% the prior week. The report also notes that testing policy changes may affect positivity rates, and that comparisons over time should be interpreted cautiously. Additionally, it mentions that influenza activity remained stable, while RSV activity increased. The data is based on the unified sample dataset (USD) and includes information on vaccine uptake, with lower rates observed among certain age groups and higher rates among pregnant women. The report was published on 29 October 2026 and is available at the provided URL.

analysis.brief_en: The World Health Organization (WHO) announced on October 27, 2026, that Sudan is launching a nationwide polio vaccination campaign targeting approximately 11 million children. The initiative, led by the Federal Ministry of Health and supported by WHO, UNICEF, and other partners, is scheduled for October–November 2026. The campaign aims to prevent the spread of polio, a disease that has been a focus of global health efforts. However, the supplied evidence does not report any confirmed or suspected outbreaks, cases, or deaths related to polio or other diseases. The WHO and its partners are actively involved in the campaign, but no specific details on the health impact or risk levels are provided. This effort is part of broader global initiatives to combat vaccine-preventable diseases.

epidemiological situation via the WHO COVID-19 dashboard. If data for certain countries is unavailable in this section, it may indicate that they have either ceased reporting COVID-19 surveillance data to WHO or have integrated the COVID-19 surveillance into existing respiratory disease surveillance. In the latter case, SARS-CoV-2 detections from sentinel and systematic virological surveillance sites in those countries may be found in the Circulation section which also includes information on SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation. This global summary of COVID-19 cases includes data on confirmed cases reported to WHO from the comprehensive COVID-19 case monitoring. Coronavirus (COVID-19) cases, %%COUNTRY%% data Source: World Health Organization Loading... Loading... Loading... What is the definition of 'confirmed' and 'reported' in COVID-19 data? All data represents the date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. In the context of WHO's statistical reporting of COVID-19 data, it is important to note that only confirmed cases are included in case and death counts. In guidance updated on 22 July 2023; there are two alternative definitions for 'Confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection' in international surveillance reporting, although some departures may exist due to local adaptations: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria OR epidemiological criteria. b) A person meeting clinical criteria AND/OR epidemiological criteria (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. Additionally, WHO only disseminates data as reported by its Member States. From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data has been compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported directly to WHO headquarters by Member States. Statistical counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. analysis.brief_en: The WHO COVID-19 dashboard provides a global summary of confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases and deaths, with data collected from countries, territories, and areas. It includes information on case definitions, testing strategies, and reporting practices, which vary by region. The dashboard has been updated since March 2020, with weekly data from July 2023 onwards. Data is subject to continuous verification and may change due to retrospective updates or shifts in reporting standards. WHO acknowledges that case detection, testing, and reporting practices differ globally, which can lead to under or overestimation of true case and death counts. Additionally, some countries have stopped reporting or changed their reporting frequency, which may affect the completeness of the data. The dashboard serves as a tool for monitoring the pandemic's spread and impact, but it is important to note that the data reflects official reports and may not capture all cases or deaths accurately.

Sanofi expands Canadians' COVID-19 vaccine choice with availability of Nuvaxovid®for the 2026-2027 respiratory season CNW Group Thu, October 29, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT 5 min read SNY +2.81% SAN -3.59% SNY +2.81% Nuvaxovid®, a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, will be available in 10 provinces and one territory for the fall 2026-2027 respiratory season A protein-based, non-mRNA vaccine that has demonstrated high efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19 in clinical trials Availability underscores Sanofi's commitment to public health and vaccine innovation in Canada TORONTO, Oct. 28, 2026 /CNW/ -- Sanofi Canada is pleased to announce that Nuvaxovid®, a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, will be available in all 10 provinces and the Yukon for the 2026-2027 season through provincial respiratory programs and most private insurers. Sanofi is the largest biopharma manufacturer in Canada, and is investing, innovating and operating across the full life sciences value chain. We are 2,000+ employees strong, invest 20% of our revenue annually in biopharma research, and are on track to deliver over $2 billion in new infrastructure investments by 2028. Sanofi is committed to our community and is working with partners to foster a long-term sustainable ecosystem and build a healthier Canada. Nuvaxovid is currently available in British Columbia, Alberta, and Quebec. In Ontario, it is expected to become available through healthcare provider offices and public health units beginning the week of October 26, 2026, with availability at pharmacies to follow. For information on availability in all provinces, individuals are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, pharmacy, or public health unit in advance to confirm vaccine availability. As a protein-based, non-mRNA option, Nuvaxovid provides Canadians with an additional vaccine option to help protect against COVID-19. As respiratory viruses begin to circulate more widely during the fall and winter months, the availability of both mRNA and non-mRNA, protein-based COVID-19 vaccines supports informed vaccine decision-making based on individual preferences and healthcare provider recommendations. "It's important for Canadians to have choice when it comes to COVID-19 vaccination and for protecting their overall health," said Michael Laclair, General Manager, Canada, Vaccines at Sanofi. "The availability of Nuvaxovid this respiratory season provides Canadians with a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine option backed by strong clinical evidence. We hope that having additional safe and effective vaccine options will encourage more Canadians to get vaccinated and help protect themselves against COVID-19 this season. Nuvaxovid reflects another step in our continued commitment to building a diverse portfolio of best-in-class vaccines to improve lives and build a healthier Canada." COVID‐19 continues to have a significant impact on Canadians, with effects that can extend far beyond the initial infection. During the 2024-2025 respiratory virus season, more than 120,000 COVID‐19 cases, 33,500 hospitalizations and 2,300 deaths were reported across Canada.1 People living with chronic conditions such as heart disease and diabetes may face a higher risk of severe COVID‐19 outcomes.2 Research also suggests that the virus may increase the risk of longer-term cardiovascular complications, including heart attack and stroke.3 Despite these risks, many Canadians remain unprotected with nearly 77% of adults not receiving a COVID‐19 vaccine during the last respiratory season.4 Story Continues Nuvaxovid is indicated for the active immunization against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) virus in individuals 12 years of age and older.5 It has been shown to have a favourable tolerability profile suitable for seasonal vaccination.6,7 The vaccine uses a well-established protein-based technology platform and has also demonstrated efficacy of approximately 90% in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 based on pivotal phase 3 clinical studies.8,9 Vaccine choice is particularly important for the approximately 5 million Canadians aged 15 years or older who live with a compromised immune system that can increase their risk of severe outcomes from COVID-19.10 These individuals are more vulnerable to complications from COVID-19 due to underlying medical conditions or treatments that can weaken the body's immune response.11 "For many immunocompromised Canadians, COVID-19 remains a significant health concern and vaccination continues to play an important role in helping reduce the risk of severe illness," said Michelle Burleigh, Co-chair, Canadian Immunocompromised Advocacy Network (CIAN). "The availability of Nuvaxovid provides another option and reflects the importance of ensuring Canadians have access to a range of vaccine choices that meet their individual needs and circumstances." Nuvaxovid is available through provincial and territorial vaccination programs in participating jurisdictions. Canadians are encouraged to get vaccinated against COVID-19 this season; they can consult their healthcare provider, pharmacist, or local public health authority for information about eligibility and vaccine availability in their region. Healthcare providers and pharmacists can contact their local health authority to obtain more information about Nuvaxovid and how to order it. We apply our deep understanding of the immune system to invent medicines and vaccines that treat and protect millions of people around the world, with an innovative pipeline that could benefit millions more. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Orbital inflammatory pseudotumor cases rose during COVID-19 Omicron wave by October 30, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Orbital inflammatory pseudotumor cases rose during COVID-19 Omicron wave Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Patients presenting with orbital disease at one hospital during the peak of the COVID-19 Omicron wave were markedly more likely to have orbital inflammatory pseudotumor than those seen in the same months of the previous three years, according to a clinical case analysis published in BMC Ophthalmology. Of 62 patients diagnosed with orbital diseases from December 2022 to January 2023, 13 cases, or 20.97 percent, involved orbital inflammatory pseudotumor, a proportion the authors report as significantly higher than in the control group drawn from the corresponding periods of the preceding three years. The study used the abbreviation OIP for orbital inflammatory pseudotumor. The researchers set out to compare the proportion of OIP among orbital disease cases during the Omicron peak with earlier years and to describe the clinical features of OIP in patients with recent COVID-19 infection. The study group comprised the 62 orbital disease patients seen during the two-month wave period, while the control group consisted of OIP patients from the same months in the previous three years, allowing a direct seasonal comparison. Discover more Get Rapid Tests Read Health News Study Anatomy The 13 OIP cases showed a consistent pattern of single-eye involvement. Six occurred in the right eye and seven in the left eye, with no apparent preference between the two sides. Eight patients were male and five were female, a slight male predominance, and ages ranged from 16 to 65, with the authors characterizing the condition as showing middle-aged prevalence in this cohort. Discover more Order Contacts Read Med Journals Find Treatments COVID-19 All cases had acute onset clinical features. Eyelid swelling and conjunctival hyperemia with chemosis were each present in 61.54 percent of patients, making them the most common signs. Ocular motility disorders affected 53.85 percent, while eye pain and diplopia each occurred in 46.15 percent. Less frequent findings included proptosis in 23.08 percent, ptosis in 15.38 percent, and decreased vision in 7.69 percent. The reported features included eyelid swelling, conjunctival hyperemia and chemosis, ocular motility disorders, eye pain, diplopia, proptosis, ptosis, and decreased vision. OIP was confirmed through ocular ultrasound, orbital CT, and MRI scans. The study reported that glucocorticoid therapy resulted in excellent treatment outcomes. Summarizing their findings, the researchers report that the proportion of OIP among orbital disease cases presenting to their hospital increased significantly from December 2022 to January 2023 compared with the corresponding periods of the preceding three years. They describe the condition in this setting as featuring single-eye onset, no significant difference between the eyes, a slightly higher incidence rate in males than females, and middle-aged prevalence, with acute onset symptoms including eyelid swelling, conjunctival hyperemia and chemosis, ocular motility disorders, and eye pain. The authors are careful to flag the limits of the evidence. The study group was relatively small, they write, and it requires further research to provide more reliable evidence. The study group consisted of 62 patients diagnosed with orbital diseases at one hospital from December 2022 to January 2023, and the control group comprised OIP patients from the same months in the previous 3 years. The authors note that the study group was relatively small and that further research is required to provide more reliable evidence.
