supplementary_news.content_title: Covid-19: Still a risk that needs to be treated quickly
supplementary_news.content: (Photo credit: SDI Productions/Getty Images) Much of the world may want COVID-19 to remain squarely in our collective rear-view mirror, but the virus — several years after initial outbreaks and treatment development — is still with us and a threat. While vaccines helped reduce severe outcomes during the pandemic, their use has declined. But the virus remains a serious threat to the people most vulnerable to it, experts warn. 1 Older people with underlying conditions remain most at risk for severe health outcomes, putting the residents of long-term care and skilled-nursing facilities in a particularly tenuous position. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 The mild illness today doesn’t predict the mild illness on day seven in this population. It’s a cascading problem. Stefan Gravenstein, MD, Brown University’s Schools of Medicine and Public Health The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates there are still millions of cases each year in the United States, hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations, and tens of thousands of deaths. 6 It’s estimated that residents of long-term care facilities account for 1 in 5 hospitalized adults older than 65 with COVID-19. 1 Further, studies have concluded that a COVID-19 infection may lead to adverse long-term health outcomes, including new-onset, heart failure, diabetes, asthma, and COPD, as well as increasing the likelihood of suffering major adverse cardiovascular events, strokes, and kidney injuries. 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 That’s why a team of doctors from Brown University wants long-term care operators and administrators to know that there are chances to intervene, to help prevent some of the worst results — if they act early enough. The clinical experts discussed the challenges and explained the steps that can be taken to mitigate potential problems during a recent McKnight’s webinar entitled, “Expert perspectives on closing the COVID-19 treatment gap in long-term care.” The team’s Health Advancement Antiviral Treatment for Long-Term Care (HEAL-LTC) program, sponsored by Pfizer, identified barriers to early intervention and has crafted tools for operators and their caretaking staffs to act sooner. “The challenge we have is that everybody thinks they know what’s going to happen if they just have the sniffles. But, in fact, the sniffles may just be the first sign,” said Stefan Gravenstein, MD, with Brown University’s Schools of Medicine and Public Health. (Photo credit: Pekic/Getty Images) Five days to act The key is to get started at the time of admission. ... Families generally just want more information. Barbara Resnick, PhD, University of Maryland School of Nursing It can take four to six days for mild symptoms to show themselves. 13 , 14 Shortness of breath and other pulmonary responses can take five to eight days. 15 , 16 , 17 Worse symptoms — the kind that can send people to the hospital and ICU for hyperinflammation — can take eight to 12 days. 13,16, 18 For that reason, the medical community has settled on a five-day window, with the clock starting at the first sign of symptoms, to effectively treat COVID-19 with oral antivirals where appropriate. Outside that five-day window, it may be too late for a treatment to make a difference. That leaves a limited amount of time to call a family member, to obtain the medication, to make dose adjustments, and more. Gravenstein likened it to a “fire drill.” Investigating hurdles to early intervention The Brown University team started its investigation by surveying 18 long-term care professionals working at four facilities across Rhode Island and interviewing five of them. All participants were directly involved with prescribing, dispensing, administering, or overseeing medication use in the facilities. Several challenges to early intervention became apparent. Early symptoms such as fatigue, confusion, and falls are common among long-term care residents. A caretaker might attribute the symptoms to some other ailment, losing critical time to treat. The time it takes to secure a family’s consent can shrink the window of treatment, not because the family is unreachable but because the urgency of the situation isn’t communicated clearly enough. The complexity of prescribing the antiviral based on other possible drug interactions and side effects and the need for alternative dosing if a resident can’t swallow pills takes time to work through if not done in advance. Preparations for ready access to medication, especially late at night or on a weekend, are often not put in place beforehand. That’s all on top of entirely reasonable pandemic fatigue leading to undertreatment of mild illnesses, as well as polypharmacy concerns and false reassurance if a resident had the virus before and did fine without treatment. The team, which included Brown University’s Rosa Baier, MPH, with the School of Public Health, and Yasin Abul, MD, with the School of Medicine, conducted a needs assessment, developing practical tools to address those needs and sharing them with two facilities to gain feedback. (Photo credit: supersizer/Getty Images) Early intervention before any symptoms The team’s resulting initiative urges that one of the first steps be taken months ahead of any possible diagnosis. Gaining the consent of a resident’s family can come as early as admission or any moment in advance when the need is less urgent. A brief family caregiver handout developed by the Brown University team, written in plain language, explains to the resident’s family why the first five days from the onset of symptoms are so critical to act. In frail adult residents, COVID rarely looks like COVID, per se. Yasin Abul, MD, Brown University School of Medicine “The key here is to get started at the time of admission,” said Barbara Resnick, PhD, RN, with the University of Maryland School of Nursing. It’s a calm time to give them options and have a discussion when there isn’t an ensuing crisis. “What the project detailed is that families generally just want more information.” The form also answers frequently asked questions, including what the adverse effects might be or why a resident would need treatment if they’ve received the vaccine. It is during these conversations that the facility can gain consent and keep it on file, at the ready for when treatment is ultimately needed. At that time, the facility’s caregivers can reach out to family to update them on the situation with consent already in hand. Staying within the treatment window By the time symptoms show up, the primary challenge is recognizing whether a resident has COVID or not, which isn’t as simple as it sounds. “In frail adult residents, COVID rarely looks like COVID, per se,” said Dr. Abul. To help, the team developed a one-page guide for nurses that has advice for signs to watch for. The “Spot It & Act Fast” guide notes several symptoms: new confusion, unexpected falls, poor oral intake, unusual sleepiness, loose stools, or family members saying the resident hasn’t been themselves. Abul knows that new confusion and falls might be mistaken for a urinary tract infection. In both cases, he urges caretakers to test for a UTI and for COVID, not one or the other. In other words, assume it’s COVID and let the provider rule it out, he said. The next step is communicating with the prescriber. A one-page Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation (or SBAR) document guides nurses in a script and decision path for when they call the medical provider, ensuring they’ve already gathered all the necessary information. Depending on what the provider decides, the guide also includes different outcomes as well as language a nurse could use to gain more clarity on why a treatment decision was made. “That call on Friday night at 9 p.m. can be so stressful for that nurse because she knows the person answering on the other end may not be so nice,” said Resnick. Finally, the team also highly encourages facilities to establish a routine workflow in advance that includes plans for having or accessing tests quickly and plans for obtaining the medicine overnight or on a weekend, as well as any known interaction concerns. Ed Davidson, PharmD, cofounder, chairman, and chief of strategy with Insight Therapeutics, reminded operators that there’s room to plan ahead for when an interaction shows up. Interactions with antivirals may be addressed by a temporary adjustment or a brief hold. “If that’s already discussed and worked out ahead of time, it lets the provider act within the treatment window instead of getting stalled,” he noted. Speedy treatment via prepped workflow The result of the team’s discussions and assessments with facility professionals is a clear pathway for treatment, helping to ensure that the treatment is made before it’s too late. They noted: It starts with providing the resident’s family easy-to-navigate information and gaining their consent for treatment. Next, it involves nurses and facility staff spotting COVID-19 symptoms and acting fast. Then, in calling the provider for their decision to treat or not, a nurse can be sure they have all the necessary information in advance and stick to a script in case they’re uncertain about communicating the resident’s needs. Finally, if following the recommended workflow, including knowing where and how to obtain the needed medicine for treatment, they will be able to treat the illness within the five-day window. Dr. Abul envisions success this way: A nurse notices a resident is a little off. The nurse tests the resident right away, then calls the provider within the hour, providing all the needed information as laid out with the SBAR-driven script. “The family already knows what’s going on because we already talked about it at admission at the beginning of care planning,” he said. Then, it’s simply a matter of getting the first dose administered in a timely manner. “All it is, is workflow.” Acting fast also determines whether COVID-19 may or may not spread among the rest of the facility’s residents. “The mild illness today doesn’t predict the mild illness on day seven in this population,” emphasized Gravenstein. “It’s a cascading problem.” ■ Havers F. The study, published in Frontiers in Public Health, recruited 20,748 participants across the three countries and is described by its authors as one of the largest multi-country community-based SARS-CoV-2 seroepidemiology studies conducted in Africa to date. The research was designed to address a puzzle that had persisted since the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic. Africa appeared to have experienced low SARS-CoV-2 infection rates and comparatively low COVID-19 morbidity and mortality, at least as measured by reported cases and deaths. Several earlier studies, however, had reported high levels of SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity among apparently healthy Africans, a discrepancy that raised two competing explanations. One possibility was that the virus had indeed spread extensively through African populations while causing relatively little severe clinical disease. The other, advanced by some researchers, was that apparent seropositivity could have resulted from pre-existing cross-reactive antibodies, antibodies raised against other coronaviruses or related pathogens that happen to bind in SARS-CoV-2 tests without reflecting true infection. To track exposure trends over time, the research teams conducted cross-sectional surveys at study sites conveniently selected within each of the three countries. Sampling was carried out during two distinct phases of the pandemic: the period when the Delta variant was dominant and the period when the Omicron variant was dominant, both nationally and globally. Discover more Study Biology Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Read Med Journals Check Symptoms Because the investigators did not perform widespread viral sequencing on participant samples, they could not attribute any individual's seropositivity to infection with a specific variant. Instead, they classified the sampling periods by whichever variant was reported as dominant at the time the samples were collected, an important methodological limitation that shapes how the results should be interpreted. Antibody detection relied on rapid diagnostic tests that measure two classes of immunoglobulins. The teams used SARS-CoV-2 IgG/IgM rapid diagnostic tests from Prestige Diagnostics at the sites in Ghana and Burkina Faso, and kits from SD Biosensor at the sites in Nigeria. These immunoassay kits had published validation procedures, and the researchers describe them as validated for the purpose of detecting SARS-CoV-2 antibodies in peripheral blood. The primary outcome of the study was the proportion of each sampled population with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, a standard measure in seroepidemiology known as seroprevalence. In addition to blood sampling, participants' demographic and clinical data were collected using a semi-structured questionnaire. This allowed the investigators to examine how seropositivity related to factors such as age and other demographic characteristics, and to record participants' vaccination status and attitudes. The headline result was the wide range of IgG seropositivity across sites, from 24.1 percent at the lowest to 76.4 percent at the highest, with higher rates observed during the Omicron-dominant period than during the Delta-dominant period. What the data do establish is that the fraction of community members with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies grew substantially between the two sampling windows across the study populations. A crucial contextual finding concerns vaccination. All study sites showed low self-reported vaccination rates, which the authors say suggests that the observed seropositivity was primarily driven by natural infection rather than by vaccine-induced antibodies. Discover more COVID-19 Read Health News Find Treatments Book Lab Tests Track Outbreaks The demographic analysis revealed a consistent pattern for age and a heterogeneous one for other factors. Across all sites, there was a significant positive association between seropositivity and age, meaning older participants were more likely to carry SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies. By contrast, the associations between seropositivity and other demographic factors were country-dependent, differing between Burkina Faso, Ghana and Nigeria. Taken together, the findings support what the authors describe as a marked disconnect between high population exposure and low reported clinical burden in the region. The study as summarized cannot adjudicate between these possibilities, since it measured antibody prevalence rather than disease outcomes, and its sites were conveniently rather than randomly selected within each country, which limits how precisely the results can be generalized to national populations. The authors argue that their results underscore the need for strengthened community-based surveillance in West Africa. SANOFI Oct 29, 2026, 07:30 ET Share this article Share this article Nuvaxovid®, a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, will be available in 10 provinces and one territory for the fall 2026-2027 respiratory season A protein-based, non-mRNA vaccine that has demonstrated high efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19 in clinical trials Availability underscores Sanofi's commitment to public health and vaccine innovation in Canada TORONTO, Oct. 28, 2026 /CNW/ -- Sanofi Canada is pleased to announce that Nuvaxovid®, a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, will be available in all 10 provinces and the Yukon for the 2026-2027 season through provincial respiratory programs and most private insurers. Nuvaxovid is currently available in British Columbia, Alberta, and Quebec. In Ontario, it is expected to become available through healthcare provider offices and public health units beginning the week of October 26, 2026, with availability at pharmacies to follow. For information on availability in all provinces, individuals are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, pharmacy, or public health unit in advance to confirm vaccine availability. As a protein-based, non-mRNA option, Nuvaxovid provides Canadians with an additional vaccine option to help protect against COVID-19. As respiratory viruses begin to circulate more widely during the fall and winter months, the availability of both mRNA and non-mRNA, protein-based COVID-19 vaccines supports informed vaccine decision-making based on individual preferences and healthcare provider recommendations. "It's important for Canadians to have choice when it comes to COVID-19 vaccination and for protecting their overall health," said Michael Laclair, General Manager, Canada, Vaccines at Sanofi. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Synthetic Sulfolipid Reshapes Dendritic Cell Response to SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein in Lab Model by October 29, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Synthetic Sulfolipid Reshapes Dendritic Cell Response to SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein in Lab Model Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A synthetic sulfolipid called Sulfavant A can reprogram how human dendritic cells respond to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in laboratory cultures, taming the inflammatory molecules the virus normally provokes while steering T cells toward regulatory and helper fates, according to a new study published in the journal Discover Immunity. The work, conducted entirely in vitro with cells from healthy donors, offers a detailed picture of an unconventional immune-activation pathway that its investigators say could eventually inform therapies for hyperinflammation, although the authors themselves caution that dampening early antiviral responses remains a real risk and that animal and clinical validation will be essential before any translational application. Sulfavant A is a synthetic glycolipid developed as a prototype for a family of small molecules that activate dendritic cells without triggering the classical inflammatory cascade. Earlier work by the same group showed that the compound engages TREM2, the triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2, and drives dendritic cell maturation characterized by upregulation of surface costimulatory molecules in the absence of inflammatory markers and cytokine release. When the engagement of TREM2 is impaired, the dendritic cell response to Sulfavant A is reduced. The researchers describe this profile as distinct from the inflammatory paradigm induced by pattern recognition receptors, the sensors such as toll-like receptors that typically ignite antiviral and inflammatory programs. The new experiments focused on a gap in that earlier picture: whether the compound could act against a viral antigen capable of evading antigen-presenting cell recognition and suppressing adaptive effector functions. The team used human monocyte-derived dendritic cells generated from peripheral blood of healthy volunteers at Umberto I Hospital of Nocera Inferiore in Salerno, Italy. Seven donor samples were used to reach statistically meaningful results, and the only exclusion criterion was prior COVID-19 vaccination, so the donors were unvaccinated at the time of blood collection. Monocytes were isolated with magnetic beads to a purity of at least 98 percent and cultured for six days with interleukin-4 and GM-CSF to yield immature dendritic cells. To mimic viral exposure, the researchers treated the cells with a commercial pool of lyophilized peptides spanning the immunodominant sequence domains of the spike glycoprotein, referred to throughout the study as SPIKE. This pool includes the receptor-binding domain, the region of the spike protein that engages the ACE2 receptor on host cells and is known to activate dendritic cells and promote their maturation. As specificity controls, parallel cultures received peptide pools covering the complete sequences of the viral membrane glycoprotein and the nucleocapsid phosphoprotein; neither of these produced measurable effects on the dendritic cells, supporting the view that the observed activity was specific to spike. After 24 hours of treatment, the contrast between the two conditions was stark. Spike peptides alone elicited minimal changes in costimulatory marker expression but markedly induced secretion of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha, the two cytokines that define the inflammatory signature of clinical SARS-CoV-2 infection. When Sulfavant A was co-administered with the spike peptides, the compound significantly upregulated the costimulatory molecules CD86, CD83, ICOSL and OX40L while reducing interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha back to basal levels. Spike stimulation did not affect HLA-DR expression, did not induce the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10 in the monocultures, and left interleukin-12 and interleukin-1 beta unchanged. The team then asked whether these dendritic cell changes would translate into altered T cell behavior. In autologous co-cultures, dendritic cells were pre-loaded with spike peptides in the presence or absence of Sulfavant A for 24 hours, the stimulus was washed away, and naive T cells from the same donor were added at a one-to-ten dendritic cell to T cell ratio. After 48 hours, the combination treatment sustained upregulation of ICOSL and OX40L, whereas spike alone selectively enhanced expression of MHC class I, CD40 and the checkpoint inhibitory molecule PD-L1, effects that Sulfavant A counteracted and restored to basal levels. Interleukin-6 secretion, elevated by spike alone, was again significantly reduced by the co-treatment, and an increase in HLA-DR was observed under the combined condition. After seven days of co-culture, proliferation measured by CFSE dilution showed that spike alone induced proliferation of CD8-positive T cells compared with untreated cultures, a response that was significantly attenuated in the presence of Sulfavant A. The compound instead promoted proliferation of a distinct CD4-positive T cell subset, and interleukin-2 was detected exclusively in the supernatants of samples treated with spike together with Sulfavant A. Flow cytometry of T cell subpopulations revealed no significant differences in Th1 or Th2 markers, but the combination expanded two defined lineages: peripheral regulatory T cells with the phenotype CD127-negative, CD4-positive, CD25-positive and FOXP3-positive, accompanied by increased interleukin-10 in the supernatants, and T follicular helper cells marked by CXCR5, BCL6 and interleukin-21, accompanied by a significant rise in interleukin-21 secretion. Cell clustering between dendritic cells and lymphocytes, a phenomenon previously associated with regulatory T cell interactions, was also evident under the combined condition. The authors interpret these results as evidence that Sulfavant A, in the presence of spike protein, promotes polarization toward both regulatory T cells and T follicular helper cells. The follicular helper lineage, mainly represented in the germinal centers of lymph nodes, is critical for activating B lymphocytes and driving antibody production, and growing evidence links this population to protective immunity induced by vaccines and to long-term protection from SARS-CoV-2. However, the researchers did not directly assess whether the expanded follicular helper cells functionally enhance B cell activation, noting that this lay beyond the scope of the study and that future investigations are planned to confirm whether the polarization translates into enhanced B cell help and antibody responses. Several important limitations frame these findings. All conclusions derive from analyses of total naive T cell populations in vitro rather than enumerated antigen-specific clones, so the results reflect population-level T cell responsiveness rather than direct evidence of spike specificity, even though the use of autologous dendritic cells pulsed with a defined viral antigen makes an antigen-driven component plausible. The study also did not directly demonstrate TREM2 dependence in this experimental setting; the observed profile is consistent with the earlier biochemical evidence that Sulfavant A binds TREM2, but other receptors or pathways may contribute, and loss-of-function studies will be required to establish the mechanism. The spike protein is known to engage TLR2 and TLR4 on myeloid cells and trigger inflammatory signaling, and the authors suggest that TREM2’s downstream pathway through DAP12, SYK and PI3K, which inhibits proinflammatory cytokine release, may contribute to the immunomodulatory effects, though this remains to be defined. The dual nature of the intervention is a recurring theme in the paper. On one hand, the reduction of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha, together with restored costimulatory signaling and a shift toward CD4-positive T cell proliferation, suggests a potential role in mitigating the immune-related adverse events of uncontrolled inflammation while preserving regulatory and helper T cell functions, with envisioned contexts ranging from vaccine adjuvants to severe COVID-19 and post-acute sequelae. On the other hand, the same regulatory activity that restrains immunopathology also reduced CD8-positive T cell expansion, and the authors acknowledge that Treg polarization and regulatory ligand expression on dendritic cells could have constrained antiviral effector functions and potentially impacted viral clearance. At present, the results are limited to in vitro models, and the researchers state that careful in vivo validation will be essential to determine whether the net effect of Sulfavant A is beneficial in specific clinical contexts. Subject of Research: Immunomodulatory effects of the synthetic sulfolipid Sulfavant A on human dendritic cell and T cell responses to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in vitro Article Title: The sulfolipid Sulfavant A modulates dendritic cell response in a cellular model of inflammation induced by SARS-CoV-2 spike protein Article References: Barra, G., Gallo, C., Manzo, E., Carbone, D., Dell’Isola, M., Affuso, M., Ziaco, M., Fioretto, L., Nuzzo, G., d’Ippolito, G., Castiglia, D., & Fontana, A. (2026). The sulfolipid Sulfavant A modulates dendritic cell response in a cellular model of inflammation induced by SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses by October 30, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A new serological study reports that acute SARS-CoV-2 infection rapidly raises antibody levels not only against the pandemic virus but also against the seasonal human coronaviruses that cause common colds. The finding, published in the journal Discover Viruses, adds to evidence that the immune response to SARS-CoV-2 departs from the classical antibody trajectory, in which immunoglobulin M appears first before the body class-switches to immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin A. That atypical pattern, the authors argue, complicates the long-standing practice of using IgM as a marker of recent infection. The research team, led by Guadalein Tanunliong and colleagues at the British Columbia public health laboratory network, analyzed serum samples from 51 people with nucleic acid amplification test-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, collected between 0 and 14 days after symptom onset, and compared them with 30 pre-pandemic control samples collected before COVID-19 first appeared in British Columbia, Canada. All 51 infected participants were tested for IgA and IgM, while 26 of the 51 available samples were also tested for IgG. The infected individuals were hospitalized patients with a median age of 68 years, and the study was conducted under a provincial mandate to validate SARS-CoV-2 serological assays for outbreak investigations and seroprevalence work. The investigators used a multiplex immunoassay, the V-PLEX Coronavirus Panel 2 from Meso Scale Discovery, to quantify antibodies against the spike proteins of the four endemic human coronaviruses, HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63, HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-OC43, as well as against the spike, nucleocapsid and receptor binding domain of ancestral SARS-CoV-2. Serum specimens were diluted 1:5000 and run on multi-spot plates with isotype-specific detection antibodies, and seropositivity thresholds were interpreted relative to validated signal cut-off values. The four endemic coronaviruses have circulated in humans since the 1960s, two of alpha lineage and two of beta lineage, and typically reinfect people every two to three years, so antibodies against them often persist at detectable levels throughout life. Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Get Allergy Relief Get Rapid Tests The results confirmed that the antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 starts early and moves fast. Serum collected at both 0 to 7 days and 8 to 14 days after onset showed higher IgA, IgG and IgM levels against SARS-CoV-2 spike, receptor binding domain and nucleocapsid than the pre-pandemic controls, with statistically significant differences. Levels trended higher at 8 to 14 days than at 0 to 7 days across all three isotypes, with the difference reaching statistical significance for IgM. Percent seropositivity also climbed over time: at 0 to 7 days, IgA seropositivity ranged from 73 to 82 percent, slightly above IgG at 56 to 78 percent and IgM at 58 to 76 percent, while by 8 to 14 days IgG seropositivity reached 100 percent for all three SARS-CoV-2 targets, exceeding IgM rates of 83 percent for nucleocapsid and 94 percent for spike and receptor binding domain. The cross-reactive signal emerged most clearly for the beta-lineage seasonal coronaviruses, HCoV-OC43 and HCoV-HKU1. IgM, IgA and IgG antibodies against these two viruses were elevated in infected individuals compared with pre-pandemic controls. At 0 to 7 days, IgM against HCoV-OC43 and IgG against HCoV-HKU1 were already significantly higher in the infected group, while other isotypes trended higher without reaching significance. By 8 to 14 days, all three isotypes against both beta coronaviruses were significantly higher in cases than controls. In contrast, most IgA and IgG responses against the alpha-lineage viruses HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63 were not significantly different between groups, although IgM against HCoV-NL63 was significantly elevated at both time points. To probe the association further, the team stratified infected individuals by their early SARS-CoV-2 antibody status. Among the 13 people who were seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 spike IgG at 0 to 7 days, the so-called early IgG responders, spike IgG levels correlated positively with IgG levels against the beta coronaviruses, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.62 for HCoV-HKU1 and 0.81 for HCoV-OC43. Among the 5 early IgG non-responders, only HCoV-NL63 showed a significant correlation, and it was negative. The authors describe these analyses as exploratory, given the small subgroup sizes, but the pattern is consistent with the idea that a rapid early IgG response to SARS-CoV-2 may reflect recall of humoral memory from prior exposure to related seasonal coronaviruses. IgM showed a parallel cross-reactive association. Among all 51 individuals tested for IgM, high SARS-CoV-2 spike IgM correlated positively with IgM against the seasonal coronavirus spike proteins during acute infection. At 0 to 7 days after onset, the correlation coefficients were highest for HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-NL63, each at 0.76, followed by HCoV-229E at 0.49 and HCoV-OC43 at 0.45. Similar correlations held at 8 to 14 days, with the exception of HCoV-OC43, which did not correlate significantly at that later window. Linear regression models for the infected groups explained a moderate share of the variability, with R-squared values between 0.21 and 0.59, and were generally stronger at 0 to 7 days for HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-NL63. Among pre-pandemic controls, by contrast, no correlation between seasonal coronavirus IgM and SARS-CoV-2 IgM was observed. Discover more Find Lung Care Study Anatomy COVID-19 Read Health News Uninterruptible power supplies An exploratory comparison of IgM to IgG ratios reinforced the picture of an IgG-dominated early response to SARS-CoV-2. Infected individuals showed significantly lower IgM:IgG ratios against SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid and spike than controls, as early as 0 to 7 days after infection, and no significant shift in the ratios occurred between the two time windows. For the seasonal coronaviruses, anti-spike IgM:IgG ratios showed no significant differences between infected individuals and controls, remaining uniformly low for HCoV-229E, HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-OC43. The exception was HCoV-NL63, where the IgM:IgG ratio was elevated in infected individuals, reaching statistical significance at 8 to 14 days, mirroring the elevated IgM levels against that virus. The study also documented baseline cross-reactivity in the pre-pandemic controls. No pre-pandemic seropositivity was observed for SARS-CoV-2 spike for any isotype, but the controls did show seropositivity for the receptor binding domain, at 17 percent for IgG, 10 percent for IgA and 13 percent for IgM, and low-level seropositivity for nucleocapsid in 3 percent for IgA and IgG. The authors note that the receptor binding domain is a smaller protein that yields lower signals and lower positivity thresholds, increasing the likelihood of false positives, and that pre-pandemic cross-reactivity rates can vary with age, year and region. The authors are careful about what the findings do and do not show. The cohort consisted of unvaccinated individuals infected with ancestral SARS-CoV-2, which the authors describe as a valuable reference point for defining early antibody kinetics without confounding from vaccination or reinfection, but the sample was small, drawn largely from hospitalized cases, and lacked clinical data on severity, comorbidities and sex-stratified analyses. There were no paired specimens for individual-level longitudinal follow-up, and the assay measured antibody quantities rather than function, so the cross-reactivity cannot be tied to neutralization or protection. The authors also cannot determine whether the early seasonal coronavirus responses reflect true antibody cross-reactivity or recall of conserved epitopes from prior exposures. Even so, they conclude that the early IgG, IgA and IgM responses to SARS-CoV-2 were associated with seasonal coronavirus responses, supporting earlier pandemic reports that IgM-based tests for recent infection are unreliable for SARS-CoV-2, and underscoring the importance of accounting for cross-reactivity when interpreting serological assays and assessing correlates of protection. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses by October 30, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A new serological study reports that acute SARS-CoV-2 infection rapidly raises antibody levels not only against the pandemic virus but also against the seasonal human coronaviruses that cause common colds. The finding, published in the journal Discover Viruses, adds to evidence that the immune response to SARS-CoV-2 departs from the classical antibody trajectory, in which immunoglobulin M appears first before the body class-switches to immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin A. That atypical pattern, the authors argue, complicates the long-standing practice of using IgM as a marker of recent infection. The research team, led by Guadalein Tanunliong and colleagues at the British Columbia public health laboratory network, analyzed serum samples from 51 people with nucleic acid amplification test-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, collected between 0 and 14 days after symptom onset, and compared them with 30 pre-pandemic control samples collected before COVID-19 first appeared in British Columbia, Canada. All 51 infected participants were tested for IgA and IgM, while 26 of the 51 available samples were also tested for IgG. The infected individuals were hospitalized patients with a median age of 68 years, and the study was conducted under a provincial mandate to validate SARS-CoV-2 serological assays for outbreak investigations and seroprevalence work. The investigators used a multiplex immunoassay, the V-PLEX Coronavirus Panel 2 from Meso Scale Discovery, to quantify antibodies against the spike proteins of the four endemic human coronaviruses, HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63, HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-OC43, as well as against the spike, nucleocapsid and receptor binding domain of ancestral SARS-CoV-2. Serum specimens were diluted 1:5000 and run on multi-spot plates with isotype-specific detection antibodies, and seropositivity thresholds were interpreted relative to validated signal cut-off values. The four endemic coronaviruses have circulated in humans since the 1960s, two of alpha lineage and two of beta lineage, and typically reinfect people every two to three years, so antibodies against them often persist at detectable levels throughout life. The results confirmed that the antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 starts early and moves fast. Serum collected at both 0 to 7 days and 8 to 14 days after onset showed higher IgA, IgG and IgM levels against SARS-CoV-2 spike, receptor binding domain and nucleocapsid than the pre-pandemic controls, with statistically significant differences. Levels trended higher at 8 to 14 days than at 0 to 7 days across all three isotypes, with the difference reaching statistical significance for IgM. Percent seropositivity also climbed over time: at 0 to 7 days, IgA seropositivity ranged from 73 to 82 percent, slightly above IgG at 56 to 78 percent and IgM at 58 to 76 percent, while by 8 to 14 days IgG seropositivity reached 100 percent for all three SARS-CoV-2 targets, exceeding IgM rates of 83 percent for nucleocapsid and 94 percent for spike and receptor binding domain. The cross-reactive signal emerged most clearly for the beta-lineage seasonal coronaviruses, HCoV-OC43 and HCoV-HKU1. IgM, IgA and IgG antibodies against these two viruses were elevated in infected individuals compared with pre-pandemic controls. At 0 to 7 days, IgM against HCoV-OC43 and IgG against HCoV-HKU1 were already significantly higher in the infected group, while other isotypes trended higher without reaching significance. By 8 to 14 days, all three isotypes against both beta coronaviruses were significantly higher in cases than controls. In contrast, most IgA and IgG responses against the alpha-lineage viruses HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63 were not significantly different between groups, although IgM against HCoV-NL63 was significantly elevated at both time points. To probe the association further, the team stratified infected individuals by their early SARS-CoV-2 antibody status. Among the 13 people who were seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 spike IgG at 0 to 7 days, the so-called early IgG responders, spike IgG levels correlated positively with IgG levels against the beta coronaviruses, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.62 for HCoV-HKU1 and 0.81 for HCoV-OC43. Among the 5 early IgG non-responders, only HCoV-NL63 showed a significant correlation, and it was negative. The authors describe these analyses as exploratory, given the small subgroup sizes, but the pattern is consistent with the idea that a rapid early IgG response to SARS-CoV-2 may reflect recall of humoral memory from prior exposure to related seasonal coronaviruses. IgM showed a parallel cross-reactive association. Among all 51 individuals tested for IgM, high SARS-CoV-2 spike IgM correlated positively with IgM against the seasonal coronavirus spike proteins during acute infection. At 0 to 7 days after onset, the correlation coefficients were highest for HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-NL63, each at 0.76, followed by HCoV-229E at 0.49 and HCoV-OC43 at 0.45. Similar correlations held at 8 to 14 days, with the exception of HCoV-OC43, which did not correlate significantly at that later window. Linear regression models for the infected groups explained a moderate share of the variability, with R-squared values between 0.21 and 0.59, and were generally stronger at 0 to 7 days for HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-NL63. Among pre-pandemic controls, by contrast, no correlation between seasonal coronavirus IgM and SARS-CoV-2 IgM was observed. An exploratory comparison of IgM to IgG ratios reinforced the picture of an IgG-dominated early response to SARS-CoV-2. Infected individuals showed significantly lower IgM:IgG ratios against SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid and spike than controls, as early as 0 to 7 days after infection, and no significant shift in the ratios occurred between the two time windows. For the seasonal coronaviruses, anti-spike IgM:IgG ratios showed no significant differences between infected individuals and controls, remaining uniformly low for HCoV-229E, HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-OC43. The exception was HCoV-NL63, where the IgM:IgG ratio was elevated in infected individuals, reaching statistical significance at 8 to 14 days, mirroring the elevated IgM levels against that virus. The study also documented baseline cross-reactivity in the pre-pandemic controls. No pre-pandemic seropositivity was observed for SARS-CoV-2 spike for any isotype, but the controls did show seropositivity for the receptor binding domain, at 17 percent for IgG, 10 percent for IgA and 13 percent for IgM, and low-level seropositivity for nucleocapsid in 3 percent for IgA and IgG. The authors note that the receptor binding domain is a smaller protein that yields lower signals and lower positivity thresholds, increasing the likelihood of false positives, and that pre-pandemic cross-reactivity rates can vary with age, year and region. The authors are careful about what the findings do and do not show. The cohort consisted of unvaccinated individuals infected with ancestral SARS-CoV-2, which the authors describe as a valuable reference point for defining early antibody kinetics without confounding from vaccination or reinfection, but the sample was small, drawn largely from hospitalized cases, and lacked clinical data on severity, comorbidities and sex-stratified analyses. There were no paired specimens for individual-level longitudinal follow-up, and the assay measured antibody quantities rather than function, so the cross-reactivity cannot be tied to neutralization or protection. The authors also cannot determine whether the early seasonal coronavirus responses reflect true antibody cross-reactivity or recall of conserved epitopes from prior exposures. Even so, they conclude that the early IgG, IgA and IgM responses to SARS-CoV-2 were associated with seasonal coronavirus responses, supporting earlier pandemic reports that IgM-based tests for recent infection are unreliable for SARS-CoV-2, and underscoring the importance of accounting for cross-reactivity when interpreting serological assays and assessing correlates of protection. A new study investigates how hydrophobic remodeling within the RBD large loop, spanning residues 475 to 490, modulates receptor engagement and spike function, offering a structural explanation for the variant’s constrained fitness. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the researchers found that A475V induces local remodeling of the receptor-binding motif and alters the geometry of the RBD–ACE2 interaction. Local refinement showed that the bulky valine substitution disrupts the interaction network surrounding residue 475, producing a 3.5-fold reduction in ACE2-binding affinity relative to BA.2.86. Unlike the L455S substitution in JN.1, which primarily alters the receptor-binding interface, A475V within the flexible large loop influences both local loop conformation and global spike conformational properties. Systematic mutagenesis identified A475 and F486 as functionally constrained hydrophobic residues that preserve the structural framework of ACE2 engagement despite extensive sequence variation in the surrounding loop. Molecular dynamics simulations and functional assays supported these structural observations, indicating that the loop tolerates sequence change only within limits set by receptor recognition and conformational stability. Discover more Read Med Journals Study Biology Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Study Chemistry The findings establish the RBD 475–490 large loop as a structurally plastic yet functionally constrained element that balances receptor recognition, conformational stability, and antigenic diversification. The authors present this as a mechanistic framework for understanding region-specific evolutionary constraints that shape SARS-CoV-2 RBD adaptation. Because the work combines structural biology, simulation, and functional testing, it links a single amino acid change to measurable effects on receptor binding and spike behavior, clarifying why JN.4 has not followed the same expansion trajectory as JN.1 despite sharing recent ancestry within the Omicron radiation. Balogun the latest to be linked 8hESPN What soccer stars did for Halloween: James the Joker, DracuLucas, more 13hChris Wright Pulisic staying in Milan reflects his club career: Good, but not quite great 2dJeff Carlisle Man United implode at Chelsea, and, make no mistake, they are in a Premier League relegation battle 1dMark Ogden Are Man City fans right about a Premier League 'Red Cartel' that's out to get them? 2dMark Ogden Ronaldo goal review: Why his 982nd career strike should be an own goal instead 2dAndy Davies Global power ranking: The top 20 soccer teams in the world, ranked! 2dRyan O'Hanlon Man City, Bayern among the good, bad and lucky in Europe's top leagues 3dBill Connelly Xhaka, Embolo to return for Switzerland after fake COVID-19 documents case play Breel Embolo gets on the scoresheet for Atlanta United FC (1:02) ESPN News Services Multiple Authors Oct 27, 2026, 12:16 PM ET Share Copy Link Email Print Granit Xhaka was restored as captain of Switzerland on Tuesday after missing four games because he admitted using fake vaccination certificates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Atlanta United forward Breel Embolo, who was further implicated in September in a similar case, also can be picked again for two Nations League matches next month, the Swiss soccer federation said in a statement. "I am pleased once again to be able to make my selections without restrictions for the November games," Switzerland coach Murat Yakin said. Yakin, his staff and players were unanimous in wanting Xhaka to continue as captain, the federation said. Xhaka revealed this month he was put on two years' probation for getting a fake vaccine document in 2022. He paid court costs with a suspended fine of 150,000 Swiss francs ($180,000). The Sunderland captain can add to his national-team record of 152 caps when Switzerland play in Slovenia on Nov. 13 and host Scotland three days later. Embolo, who joined MLS side Atlanta United in August, has 26 goals in 92 appearances for the Swiss. World Cup quarterfinalists Switzerland top their Nations League second-tier group, five points ahead of Slovenia, seeking promotion back to the top tier. Services will restart on Thursday, September 9. The Iloilo provincial capitol announced on Tuesday, September 7, a temporary shutdown of services after 15 personnel tested positive for COVID-19. Provincial Administrator Suzette Mamon said the move would allow “maximum contact tracing and disinfection.” Services will restart on Thursday, September 9. On the other side of Western Visayas, Negros Occidental provincial officials were eyeing levels of lockdown of two hospitals after a doctor and a nurse tested positive for COVID-19. A doctor from the Teresita Jalandoni Provincial Hospital in Silay City was taken from an isolation center to the Corazon Locsin Montelibano Memorial Hospital because of worsening symptoms, the province’s COVID-19 task force announced. A nurse from a different hospital was already recovering. The Don Jose S. Monfort Medical Center Extension Hospital in Barotac Nuevo, Iloilo, also temporarily suspended elective surgeries until September 13 to conduct contact tracing and disinfection. It did not give any figures for infected staff. In Iloilo City, Mayor Jerry Treñas said three priests, a cook, and a secretary of a church in La Paz district had also tested positive for the virus. The mayor did not give details but Aksyon Radyo Iloilo said 31 personnel of the church are under quarantine. Treñas on Tuesday added seven more barangays to the local granular lockdown list, bringing to 36 the number of areas where egress and ingress – except by health officials – will be banned for 72 hours. Areas are placed under granular lockdown if there are two or more COVID-19 cases. The mayor assured communities that affected households would receive food and other aid. The lockdown involves mandatory reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) tests of close contacts and contact tracing for second tier contacts. Iloilo City recorded 159 new COVID-19 cases on Monday, September 6, and 105 the day before. “Our cases keep rising so please stay at home and get yourselves vaccinated,” the mayor urged. Must Read Slow delivery of vaccines blamed for COVID-19 deaths in Bacolod, Iloilo COVID-19 cases also kept rising in Negros Occigental, where Governor Eugenio Jose “Bon” Lacson said active cases have once more surged past the 1,000 mark. Bacolod City, meanwhile, reported two new Delta cases, including a hospital healthcare worker, tracing 11 close contacts and putting them on lockdown until their test results come out. Lacson said the most affected cities in the province are Bago, just south of Bacolod, E.B. Magalona in the province’s middle northern part, and San Carlos City in the far north. Local executives also had good news for constituents. Treñas announced free RT-PCR tests at the city’s Jubilee Hall for all symptomatic patients and their contacts, returning overseas Filipinos, and returning residents. He also asked the city council to put a P1,800 cap on the price of RT-PCR tests to help businesses that need to continuously test employees. The mayor said residents need a doctor’s referral to get free tests. “Those who will undergo a swab test for travel or employment purposes will be charged with the current rate of P2,500 pending the amendment in the ordinance,” Treñas said. The Philippine Red Cross also announced a price drop for RT-PCR tests. It slashed the price of its swab test by a thousand pesos, from P3,800 to P2,800. The price for the saliva-based test is now P1,500, from P2,000. Bacolod City Administrator Em Ang reported the launch of the city’s fourth vaccination bus and a return to workplace inoculation, saying it would help speed up goals to achieve herd immunity. – Rappler.com Add to Preferred Sources Share in Chat Share article Facebook X (Twitter) Copy Link Copied How does this make you feel? supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Teenager with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS recovers after a year of multifaceted care, case report says by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Teenager with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS recovers after a year of multifaceted care, case report says Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A 17-year-old high-school student who became bedridden for more than half of each day after a SARS-CoV-2 infection has made a full recovery from post-COVID-19 myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, according to a case report published in BioPsychoSocial Medicine on 10 September 2026. The report, authored by Takakazu Oka, describes how the patient, who had already received treatments at other medical facilities without returning to school, was ultimately able to enter university approximately one year after her initial consultation. Post-COVID-19 ME/CFS is a condition in which some people infected with SARS-CoV-2 develop persistent fatigue and cognitive dysfunction that meet the diagnostic criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome. The report notes that no established treatment exists for this condition, and that accounts of patients who have recovered remain limited. Because the pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying the disabling symptoms are not yet fully understood, the author adopted a multifaceted treatment approach that considered disease severity, functional level, illness beliefs and coping behaviors, social support systems, comorbidities, secondary issues, and the phase of recovery. The treatment programme described in the case presentation comprised ten components introduced progressively and tailored to the patient’s phase of recovery. These were instruction on eating habits and supplements; instruction on physical activities; instruction on managing cognitive fatigue; environmental adjustment; pharmacotherapy with midodrine, ibudilast, and the traditional Japanese herbal medicines hochuekkito and tokishakuyakusan; facilitation of therapeutic interoceptive awareness; adjustment of disrupted diurnal sleep-wake rhythms; conditioning exercise; instructions for safe recovery; and nurturing self-efficacy. Discover more Find Treatments Get Health Tips Book Care Services Get Rapid Tests According to the report, the patient was referred to the author’s department for severe fatigue that developed after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Despite treatments at other facilities, she remained bedridden for more than half of each day and was unable to attend school. After the progressive, multiperspective interventions, the report states that approximately one year after her initial consultation she made a full recovery, entered university, and is now enjoying university life. The author concludes that the report describes, in detail, the evaluation and multifaceted treatment of a 17-year-old high-school student with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS who had been unable to attend school but who ultimately recovered and was able to attend university. As a single-patient case report, the findings describe one individual’s course of care and cannot by themselves establish the efficacy of any component of the treatment approach for post-COVID-19 ME/CFS more broadly, a limitation consistent with the report’s own observation that no established treatment exists and that recovery reports remain limited. The article was published as an open-access case report and, at the time of this writing, was shared as an early, peer-reviewed accepted version subject to further edits before the final version of record. Image Courtesy: Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar HEALTHCARE Create Bookmark RSV poses greater risk of hospitalization for children than flu or COVID-19, Qatar study finds The findings underscore the importance of strengthening preventive strategies Press Release Doha – Researchers at Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar (WCM-Q) and Sidra Medicine, in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health and Hamad Medical Corporation, have found that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) was associated with substantially more severe illness than influenza or COVID-19 among children in Qatar. The findings underscore the importance of strengthening preventive strategies, including increasing vaccination uptake and expanding access to long-acting monoclonal antibodies against RSV, to reduce the burden of severe respiratory illness among children. Published in the prestigious journal The Lancet Regional Health – Eastern Mediterranean, the study analyzed a large, systematically collected dataset comprising 4,360 respiratory illness episodes among 3,932 children younger than 18 years who attended Sidra Medicine’s emergency department between January 2022 and December 2025. Sidra Medicine serves as Qatar’s national referral center for specialized pediatric care. The study encompassed the entire pediatric age spectrum, from infancy through adolescence, and assessed disease severity based on hospitalization and intensive care unit admission. The study is the first from the Eastern Mediterranean Region to directly compare the severity of RSV, influenza, and COVID-19 across the full pediatric age spectrum, from infancy through adolescence. By examining all three viruses over four years of concurrent circulation within a single national pediatric referral setting, the study addresses important limitations of previous research worldwide, which has often been restricted to comparisons between two viruses, specific age groups, or different periods of viral circulation. These findings make an important contribution to the international evidence base while providing much-needed regional evidence to inform clinical care, public health strategies, and immunization policies. The study found that RSV was associated with substantially more severe illness than either influenza or COVID-19, while the latter two infections showed broadly similar severity. Influenza accounted for 65% of the illness episodes studied, followed by COVID-19 at 22% and RSV at just 13%. Despite its smaller share of illnesses, hospital admission was approximately four times as common with RSV as with either of the other infections, and intensive care admission was more than three times as common. This pattern remained after accounting for differences in patient characteristics and was consistent across age groups, although RSV predominantly affected younger children. Dr. Andres Perez-Lopez, Chief of the Microbiology Division at Sidra Medicine, who co-led the study and oversaw its microbiological and clinical components, said: “One of the most striking findings was how strongly a child’s underlying health influenced the severity of respiratory infections. Children with pre-existing medical conditions had nearly seven times greater chances of hospitalization and twelve times greater chances of requiring intensive care compared with children without these conditions. These findings highlight the importance of identifying vulnerable children early and ensuring they receive appropriate monitoring, preventive care, and medical care.” Dr. Hiam Chemaitelly, Assistant Professor of Research in Population Health Sciences at WCM-Q, who designed and co-led the study and oversaw its epidemiological component, said: “It was striking to see how frequently RSV led to hospitalization and how much could be gained through prevention. Fortunately, effective interventions are now available, including RSV vaccination during pregnancy to protect newborns and long-acting monoclonal antibodies that protect infants during their most vulnerable early months. Increasing uptake of these interventions, supported by conversations with families during routine pregnancy care, could help prevent severe illness and avoidable hospitalizations. Equally important is improving influenza and COVID-19 vaccination uptake among children, as these infections can also cause serious illness. Raising awareness among families and encouraging the use of these preventive measures are essential to protecting children’s health.” The study, titled “Relative severity of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus among pediatric emergency department attendees in Qatar: a retrospective cohort study,” was supported by the Qatar Research, Development and Innovation Council through grant ARG02-0402-240119. Collaborators included Qatar’s Ministry of Public Health, and Hamad Medical Corporation. About Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar is a partnership between Cornell University and Qatar Foundation. It offers a comprehensive Six-Year Medical Program leading to the Cornell University M.D. degree with teaching by Cornell and Weill Cornell faculty and by physicians at Hamad Medical Corporation (HMC), Sidra Medicine, the Primary Health Care Corporation, and Aspetar Orthopedic and Sports Medicine Hospital, who hold Weill Cornell appointments. Through its biomedical research program, WCM-Q is building a sustainable research community in Qatar while advancing basic science and clinical research. supplementary_news.content: Monday, November 02, 2026 PDF Supplements Go Top Stories Qatar Business Sport World Gulf/(MiddleEast) Press Release Latest News Health/Medicine Lifestyle/Fashion Science/Tech Cinema/Showbiz Home / Nation / RSV poses greater hospitalisation risk for children than influenza or COVID-19, Qatar study finds RSV poses greater hospitalisation risk for children than influenza or COVID-19, Qatar study finds 29/10/2026 / Nation Research by Dr. Andres Perez-Lopez of Sidra Medicine and Dr. Hiam Chemaitelly of WCM-Q has provided new evidence on the relative severity of RSV, influenza, and COVID-19 among children in Qatar. + A A - Qatar tribune Tribune News Network Doha Researchers at Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar (WCM-Q) and Sidra Medicine, in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health and Hamad Medical Corporation, have found that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) was associated with substantially more severe illness than influenza or COVID-19 among children in Qatar. The findings underscore the importance of strengthening preventive strategies, including increasing vaccination uptake and expanding access to long-acting monoclonal antibodies against RSV to reduce the burden of severe respiratory illness among children. Published in the prestigious journal The Lancet Regional Health – Eastern Mediterranean, the study analysed a large, systematically collected dataset comprising 4,360 respiratory illness episodes among 3,932 children younger than 18 years who attended Sidra Medicine’s emergency department between January 2022 and December 2025. Sidra Medicine serves as Qatar’s national referral centre for specialised paediatric care. The study is the first from the Eastern Mediterranean Region to directly compare the severity of RSV, influenza, and COVID-19 across the full paediatric age spectrum, from infancy through adolescence. By examining all three viruses over four years of concurrent circulation within a single national paediatric referral setting, the study addresses important limitations of previous research worldwide, which has often been restricted to comparisons between two viruses, specific age groups, or different periods of viral circulation. These findings make an important contribution to the international evidence base while providing much-needed regional evidence to inform clinical care, public health strategies, and immunisation policies. The study found that RSV was associated with substantially more severe illness than either influenza or COVID-19, while the latter two infections showed broadly similar severity. Influenza accounted for 65% of the illness episodes studied, followed by COVID-19 at 22% and RSV at just 13%. Despite its smaller share of illnesses, hospital admission was approximately four times as common with RSV as with either of the other infections, and intensive care admission was more than three times as common. This pattern remained after accounting for differences in patient characteristics and was consistent across age groups, although RSV predominantly affected younger children. Dr. Andres Perez-Lopez, chief of the Microbiology Division at Sidra Medicine, who co-led the study and oversaw its microbiological and clinical components, said: “One of the most striking findings was how strongly a child’s underlying health influenced the severity of respiratory infections. Children with pre-existing medical conditions had nearly seven times greater chances of hospitalisation and twelve times greater chances of requiring intensive care compared with children without these conditions. These findings highlight the importance of identifying vulnerable children early and ensuring they receive appropriate monitoring, preventive care, and medical care.” Dr. Hiam Chemaitelly, assistant professor of Research in Population Health Sciences at WCM-Q, who designed and co-led the study and oversaw its epidemiological component, said: “It was striking to see how frequently RSV led to hospitalisation and how much could be gained through prevention. Fortunately, effective interventions are now available, including RSV vaccination during pregnancy to protect newborns and long-acting monoclonal antibodies that protect infants during their most vulnerable early months. Increasing uptake of these interventions, supported by conversations with families during routine pregnancy care, could help prevent severe illness and avoidable hospitalisations. Equally important is improving influenza and COVID-19 vaccination uptake among children, as these infections can also cause serious illness.” The study, titled “Relative severity of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus among paediatric emergency department attendees in Qatar: a retrospective cohort study,” was supported by the Qatar Research, Development and Innovation Council through grant ARG02-0402-240119. Collaborators included Qatar’s Ministry of Public Health, and Hamad Medical Corporation. Copy 29/10/2026 40

Healthcare Workers: Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月31日 来源:Health Science Reports 2.9 编辑推荐: 背景与目的 COVID-19可导致感染后持续存在的症状,即所谓的长新冠(Long COVID)。本研究旨在明确经确诊的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2型(SARS-CoV-2)感染者以及医护人员中持续性体征和症状的患病率。 方法 本研究为系统综述与Meta分析,遵 免费下载【类器官培养与鉴定指南】,帮您快速选择不同类器官培养所需的细胞因子和标志物抗体。 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW Open Access 背景与目的 COVID-19可导致感染后持续存在的症状,即所谓的长新冠(Long COVID)。本研究旨在明确经确诊的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2型(SARS-CoV-2)感染者以及医护人员中持续性体征和症状的患病率。 方法 本研究为系统综述与Meta分析,遵循系统综述和Meta分析首选报告条目(PRISMA)指南,并已在国际前瞻性系统综述注册库(PROSPERO)注册(注册号:CRD42023460632)。纳入标准为COVID-19感染后随访时间至少12周的队列研究。检索于2023年11月在PubMed、Scopus、Embase、Scielo及LILACS/BVS数据库以及灰色文献中进行。采用Rayyan软件进行文献筛选,并在R软件中对各症状进行合并患病率Meta分析。方法学质量采用纽卡斯尔-渥太华量表(NOS)进行评估。 结果 共检索到2,456项研究,其中59篇文献纳入系统综述,58篇纳入Meta分析,涉及196,863名参与者。合并患病率(95%置信区间[CI])最高的症状为疲劳(0.29[0.24–0.36],95%预测区间[PI]:0.05–0.78)和呼吸困难(0.16[0.12–0.22],95% PI:0.01–0.71)。 结论 医护人员在部分持续性症状(疲劳、呼吸困难、咳嗽、味觉改变及胃肠道症状)上的患病率低于普通人群。多数研究质量为中等。尽管研究发现持续性症状的患病率较高,但高异质性仍是主要局限性。 论文主体内容总结 索取CAR-T 细胞免疫疗法最新资料领 取 1 引言 COVID-19由SARS-CoV-2病毒引起,全球已导致超过7.75亿例感染和700余万例死亡。急性期主要累及呼吸系统,表现为咳嗽、呼吸困难、流涕和咽痛等症状,亦可出现胃肠道、肌肉骨骼、神经、发热、嗅觉与味觉功能障碍及心脏表现。疾病严重程度差异显著,部分患者症状轻微,部分则需住院治疗及出院后随访。疫情进展中逐渐认识到该病可导致长期系统性受累,即持续性症状与后遗症,被称为新冠后综合征或长新冠。英国国家健康与临床优化研究所(NICE)与世界卫生组织(WHO)将其定义为感染急性期后症状持续超过3个月(12周)且无法以其他诊断解释的状况。最常见的持续性症状包括疲劳、呼吸困难、肌痛、头痛、嗅觉与味觉丧失及运动不耐受。医护人员长期处于抗疫一线,面临工作流程改变和照护后勤调整,加之个人防护装备(PPE)短缺,感染风险升高。据此提出研究问题:普通人群和医护人员中SARS-CoV-2感染所致的持续性体征和症状中哪些最为普遍?本研究旨在明确感染普通人群及医护人员中COVID-19持续性体征和症状的患病率。 2 材料与方法 2.1 设计 本研究为系统文献综述与Meta分析,遵循PRISMA原则,并于2023年9月5日在PROSPERO注册(编号CRD42023460632)。该方案亦支持已发表的关于COVID-19心理与认知后遗症的系统综述,两项综述目标与结局不同,检索策略和纳入标准共享,但数据提取和Meta分析分别独立进行。 2.2 检索方法 于2023年11月在PubMed、Scopus、Embase、Scielo和LILACS/BVS数据库中进行检索,并辅以纳入研究参考文献列表的手工检索和灰色文献检索。采用健康科学描述符(DeCS)和医学主题词表(MeSH)中的“Post-Acute COVID-19 Syndrome”“Long COVID”“Cohort Studies”等术语,结合布尔运算符OR和AND构建各数据库检索策略。采用PECOs策略:人群(P)为普通人群和医护人员;暴露(E)为SARS-CoV-2感染;无对照组(C);结局(O)为持续性COVID-19体征和症状;研究类型(s)为观察性队列研究。 2.3 纳入与排除标准 纳入经聚合酶链反应(PCR)或抗原检测确诊SARS-CoV-2感染、且依据WHO和NICE定义评估感染后持续性症状的纵向观察性队列研究。排除仅凭临床评估或疑似病例诊断的研究、基于血清学诊断且无法估计感染后随访时间的研究、纯儿科人群、感染后随访不足3个月或随访时间不明的研究,以及数据不足且作者在两次联系后1个月内未回复的研究。 2.4 数据处理 检索结果导入Endnote去除重复文献,其余文献上传至Rayyan,由两名独立评审者进行筛选,分歧经协商解决,无法达成一致时由第三名专家裁定。评审者间一致性采用kappa统计量评估。筛选完成后将数据导出至作者设计的Excel表格,提取研究标识、样本特征及COVID-19诊断后随访时长等变量。当随访时间以范围报告时,取中点值归入分析组,可能导致随访时长分类偏差。 2.5 检索结局 研究结局为持续性COVID-19体征和症状,初始逐项提取且不进行数据填补,信息缺失时联系作者。为便于Meta分析,临床相关结局归入预定义症状类别(疲劳:疲劳、疲倦、虚弱、体能下降和运动不耐受;心悸:心悸和心动过速)。同一类别内报告多个结局时仅纳入单一估计值以避免重复计数,并选取患病率最高者。 2.6 数据提取 Meta分析在R软件4.4.1版本中使用“meta”包7.0-0版本进行,采用随机效应模型和逆方差法。合并前进行logit转换,研究间方差(τ2)采用限制性最大似然(REML)法估计。各持续性症状分别以95%置信区间进行患病率Meta分析。异质性采用Q检验和I2不一致指数计算,显著性水平设为p≤0.05。I2≤25%视为同质,>25%且<75%为中度异质性,≥75%为高度异质性。鉴于所有结局均呈现高异质性,依据参与者是否为医护人员、感染后随访时间、队列类型、研究地点、住院状态和研究质量进行亚组分析。未进行敏感性分析,理由是纳入研究存在临床和方法学异质性,剔除单项研究不太可能实质性改变总体结果。 2.7 质量评价 采用适用于队列研究的纽卡斯尔-渥太华量表(NOS)评估方法学质量,该量表涵盖参与者选择、组间可比性及结局和随访评估三个领域。依据总分将研究分为差(0–3星)、中等(4–6星)和良好(7–9星)。采用Egger检验和漏斗图评估各结局的发表偏倚。未进行证据确定性评估,因纳入研究均为疫情背景下的队列研究,假定存在较高偏倚风险。 3 结果 文献检索共获得2,456篇相关文章,去除1,229篇重复文献后,经标题和摘要筛选,203篇进行全文评估,其中141篇因不符合纳入/排除标准或数据提取不足被排除,4篇因属同一队列被排除,1篇无法获取全文,灰色文献中纳入1篇。最终59篇纳入系统综述,其中58篇进入定量分析,1篇因仅报告单一未纳入定量分析的结局而被排除。系统综述总人群为196,863名参与者。kappa指数为κ=0.792(p<0.001),表明一致性较好。58篇Meta分析文献中,6篇专门针对医护人员,2篇同时包含医护人员和普通人群并进行分层分析,故共8项研究涉及医护人员。多数研究为前瞻性队列(81.4%),质量以中等为主(89.8%)。样本量从27人到127,859人不等。普通人群平均年龄为31.3至71岁,医护人员为34.4至42.2岁。随访期从感染确诊后3至24个月不等。地理分布上,多数研究来自欧洲(32项),其次为南美洲和北美洲(各9项)、亚洲(7项)、非洲(1项),另有1项跨欧洲和南美洲的多国研究。Meta分析合并患病率(95%CI)最高的结局依次为:疲劳(0.29[0.24;0.36],95% PI:0.05–0.78,I2=98.9%)、呼吸困难(0.16[0.12;0.22],95% PI:0.01–0.71,I2=99.5%)、关节痛(0.12[0.07;0.19],95% PI:0.01–0.72,I2=97.8%)、肌痛(0.11[0.07;0.16],95% PI:0.01–0.59,I2=98.4%)、头痛(0.10[0.07;0.13],95% PI:0.01–0.53,I2=99.5%)、脱发(0.09[0.06;0.13],95% PI:0.01–0.42,I2=98.7%)、嗅觉功能障碍(0.08[0.06;0.12],95% PI:0.01–0.45,I2=97.2%)和心悸(0.08[0.05;0.12],95% PI:0.01–0.49,I2=98.4%)。患病率较低的结局包括咳嗽、头晕/昏厥、胸痛/胸闷、味觉改变、胃肠道症状、皮肤改变和发热/寒战。亚组分析显示,医护人员在疲劳、呼吸困难、咳嗽、味觉改变和胃肠道症状上的合并患病率显著低于普通人群(p<0.05),其中味觉改变和胃肠道症状在医护人员中的异质性显著降低(I2<25%)。随访时间未显示症状患病率的显著差异。地理因素对多数结局有显著影响,但可能受欧洲、南美和北美研究集中的影响。前瞻性研究在疲劳、头痛、心悸、咳嗽和胃肠道症状上的患病率高于回顾性研究。住院状态与呼吸困难、咳嗽、心悸和头晕/昏厥四种症状的差异显著相关,咳嗽在住院患者中更为普遍。 4 讨论 本系统综述结果表明,确诊SARS-CoV-2感染的个体在急性疾病消退后仍经历持续性症状,可能影响其生活质量、日常活动、返岗复工,并给医疗系统带来额外负担。预测区间较宽与研究间高异质性一致,结果应谨慎解读。异质性可能反映研究人群、住院状态、随访时长、流行病毒变异株、疫苗接种状态、症状确定方法和地理差异等方面的不同。疲劳是最普遍的症状(合并患病率为0.29),可能与免疫失调和细胞能量代谢改变有关,包括线粒体功能受损。持续性呼吸困难和咳嗽是临床关注重点,可能源于病毒所致的残余肺损伤或炎症。肌肉骨骼症状如肌痛和关节痛可能反映持续的炎症状态。嗅觉和味觉功能障碍在急性期常见,其持续存在与认知损害相关。皮肤问题如皮疹和脱发亦较常见,尤其在女性中。头痛为第五常见症状,可见于有无头痛病史的个体。心血管症状如胸痛和心悸在感染期间和感染后均有报道。胃肠道症状和发热/寒战患病率较低,可能并非新冠后综合征的核心特征。亚组分析中,医护人员在疲劳、呼吸困难、咳嗽、味觉改变和胃肠道症状上的患病率显著较低,可能反映其优先获得疫苗接种、平均年龄较年轻、症状报告不足或早期识别和治疗等因素,但这些解释应视为假设而非因果推断。漏斗图不对称性提示疲劳、肌痛、脱发和发热/寒战的合并患病率估计可能受报告偏倚影响,应谨慎解读。 5 优势与局限性 本研究的优势在于同时分析多个结局(15种症状),可识别患病率最高者,且样本广泛且稳健。主要局限性包括依赖自我报告症状,可能受主观感知影响导致低估或高估;许多研究纳入住院或门诊患者,急性期症状较重者可能具有更高的感染后症状患病率,无症状或轻症个体可能代表性不足;疫情背景下研究的方法学和人群差异可能导致高异质性;部分结局存在小研究效应,提示可能存在发表偏倚。 打赏 展开全文 supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Folic acid food fortification linked to lower COVID-19 incidence in country-level analysis by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Folic acid food fortification linked to lower COVID-19 incidence in country-level analysis Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Countries that mandate folic acid fortification of foods reported substantially lower COVID-19 incidence than countries without such policies, according to a peer-reviewed study published in BMC Public Health. In analyses stratified by World Health Organization region, mandatory fortification in Africa and Europe was associated with roughly 70 percent lower COVID-19 incidence, while no statistically significant association emerged for mortality. The research team, led by Wendy N. Nembhard and colleagues, set out to test a hypothesis that circulated widely during the pandemic: that SARS-CoV-2 might co-opt folate metabolism to support viral replication. Some earlier studies had suggested that folic acid supplementation could decrease the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection while potentially increasing the risk of death after infection, prompting the authors to examine whether population-level folic acid intake through food fortification was associated with COVID-19 outcomes at the country level. To conduct the analysis, the team drew country-specific data on folic acid fortification policy status, the extent of grain fortification, and total adjusted potential folic acid food intake from the Global Fortification Data Exchange. COVID-19 incidence and mortality data covering December 2019 through April 2023 came from the World Health Organization. Countries were grouped into WHO regions and World Bank income classes to account for the enormous differences in health systems, demographics, and pandemic trajectories across the globe. The statistical approach centered on negative binomial regression, a model suited to count data such as infection and death counts, which the researchers used to estimate rate ratios and 95 percent confidence intervals for COVID-19 incidence and mortality per 100,000 population. These estimates were stratified by region and income group, allowing the authors to compare fortification status within, rather than across, broadly similar groupings of countries. Discover more food fortification Explore Food Tech Order Vitamins COVID-19 Get Rapid Tests Because countries that fortify foods differ systematically from those that do not, in wealth, age structure, population size, and geography, the researchers also performed propensity score analyses. These models adjusted for gender and age distribution, population size, country-level income, and geographical region, attempting to mimic the balance of a controlled experiment by comparing fortification and non-fortification countries that were otherwise similar on measured characteristics. The headline result held in both Africa and Europe: countries with mandatory folic acid fortification policies had approximately 70 percent lower COVID-19 incidence than countries without such policies, with a rate ratio of 0.26 in Africa (95 percent confidence interval 0.11 to 0.60) and 0.27 in Europe (95 percent confidence interval 0.13 to 0.57). When the propensity score models pooled countries across regions and adjusted for income and other covariates, the difference in COVID-19 incidence between fortification and non-fortification countries remained statistically significant. Mortality told a different story. Across the analyses, including the propensity score models, the researchers found no statistically significant association between folic acid fortification and COVID-19 mortality. The authors concluded that folic acid fortification was associated with lower COVID-19 incidence after adjusting for income and region, but not with mortality, and they emphasized that additional studies are needed to investigate the association further. The study's design carries important limitations that the authors and readers must weigh. This is an ecological, country-level comparison rather than a study of individuals, so it cannot establish that folic acid intake caused any person's infection risk to fall. Unmeasured differences between countries, from testing capacity and reporting practices to pandemic timing and public health measures, could contribute to the observed patterns, and the fortification exposure reflects potential intake at the population level rather than measured individual consumption. The findings therefore stand as an observational signal, one that the researchers say warrants further investigation rather than a demonstration of protective effect.
