supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Gum Disease Inflammation Activates Viral Entry Pathways Tied to SARS-CoV-2 by October 27, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Gum Disease Inflammation Activates Viral Entry Pathways Tied to SARS-CoV-2 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram SARS-CoV-2 is best known as a respiratory pathogen, but the oral cavity has increasingly drawn attention as a site where viral activity, receptor expression, microbial communities, and inflammation intersect. A new study published open access in BMC Infectious Diseases on 26 October 2026 reports that periodontal disease, a chronic dysbiotic inflammatory condition of the tissues supporting the teeth, is associated with heightened activity of a non-canonical viral entry pathway that SARS-CoV-2 can potentially exploit. The research, led by Afsar Naqvi and colleagues, focused on the phosphatidylserine, or PS, dependent entry route, which involves the TIM family of receptors and related enzymes, and asked whether the inflamed gum environment characteristic of periodontitis primes this pathway. The team examined expression of genes belonging to the PS-dependent pathway, including ADAM17, ATP11c, TIM1, TIM3, and TIM4, across three settings: gingival tissue, saliva, and human oral keratinocytes grown in the laboratory. In prepandemic gum biopsy samples, inflamed periodontal tissue showed significant upregulation of all of these non-canonical receptors compared with healthy tissue. According to the authors, this indicates that periodontal disease on its own establishes a molecular environment associated with PS-mediated microbial entry markers, independent of any exposure to SARS-CoV-2. The researchers then turned to a post-vaccination cohort to look for the same molecular patterns in a clinical context. Salivary expression of the PS-dependent pathway genes was markedly elevated in individuals who tested positive for COVID-19 and also had periodontal disease. These same individuals showed significantly increased levels of phosphatidylserine in their saliva. The authors interpret this as a co-occurring pattern of viral exposure and periodontal inflammation rather than proof that gum disease causes infection, and they frame the relationship as an association between COVID-19 and periodontal disease with implications for viral activity, immune dysregulation, and long-term oral health. To probe the mechanism more directly, the group performed in vitro experiments using primary human oral keratinocytes, the epithelial cells that line the mouth. When these cells were exposed to SARS-CoV-2 together with periodontal pathogens, specifically Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, the combination induced robust and concordant activation of PS-dependent entry genes, with the TIM family receptors showing particularly strong responses. This laboratory finding suggests that the co-presence of the virus and periodontal bacteria can drive the same molecular program observed in patient tissues, although results from cultured cells do not by themselves demonstrate that this occurs in the human body or that it increases actual viral infectivity. The study's design carries important limitations that shape how the findings should be read. The human data are observational: the prepandemic biopsies establish that inflamed gum tissue expresses more PS-pathway genes, and the cohort data show that COVID-19-positive individuals with periodontal disease carry higher salivary levels of those genes and of phosphatidylserine, but neither result establishes a causal chain from gum inflammation to viral entry. The in vitro work demonstrates pathway activation under controlled co-exposure conditions rather than measured enhancement of SARS-CoV-2 infection. The published version is also an early-share, peer-reviewed accepted manuscript that remains subject to further edits before the final version of record appears. Even with those caveats, the work adds a specific molecular dimension to evidence linking oral health and COVID-19. Rather than invoking general inflammation alone, the study identifies a defined receptor system, the PS/TIM axis, whose components are measurably elevated in diseased gum tissue, in the saliva of co-affected patients, and in oral epithelial cells challenged with both the virus and periodontal bacteria. The authors suggest that this inflammatory environment co-occurs with molecular conditions related to SARS-CoV-2 infection pathways in the oral mucosa, positioning periodontal status as a potential modifier of susceptibility at the viral entry surface itself. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Chemistry Compound from Algerian Desert Plant Shows Antifungal Activity and SARS-CoV-2 Binding in Lab Tests by October 29, 2026 in Chemistry Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Compound from Algerian Desert Plant Shows Antifungal Activity and SARS-CoV-2 Binding in Lab Tests Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Chemists have isolated a pentacyclic triterpenoid compound from the aerial parts of Launaea arborescens, a shrub widely distributed in southwestern Algeria, and report that it inhibits the growth of several Candida fungal species in laboratory assays while also showing favorable computed binding to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease. The compound, abbreviated HIHPT for heptamethyl–icosahydropicene–triol, was identified as 4,4,6b,8a,11,11,14b-heptamethyl-1,2,3,4,4a,5,6,6a,6b,7,8,8a,9,10,11,12,12a,14,14a,14b-icosahydropicene-3,5,8-triol, a molecule carrying three hydroxyl groups on a five-ring carbon skeleton. The extraction began with powdered, dehydrated aerial parts of the plant processed through a Soxhlet apparatus using solvents of increasing polarity: diethyl ether, dichloromethane, ethyl acetate, and n-butanol. The dichloromethane extract showed the highest biological activity among the crude fractions and was therefore selected for purification. Silica gel column chromatography with chloroform/petroleum ether and chloroform/methanol gradient elution yielded five fractions, and the bioactive compound was isolated from the fifth fraction as a white powder melting at 62 to 63 degrees Celsius. Spectroscopic characterization by infrared, proton and carbon nuclear magnetic resonance, and mass spectrometry established the molecular formula C29H48O3, with elemental analysis closely matching the calculated carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen percentages. The antifungal evaluation used five clinical fungal isolates obtained from the Microbiology Laboratory of the University Hospital of Annaba, Algeria: Candida albicans, Candida krusei, Candida kefyr, Candida lusitaniae, and Candida tropicalis. Susceptibility was determined by the agar well diffusion method following Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidelines. A stock solution of 5 milligrams of HIHPT per milliliter of dimethyl sulfoxide was prepared freshly under sterile conditions, and 20 microliters were dispensed into 6-millimeter wells punched into Sabouraud Dextrose Agar plates seeded with fungal suspensions adjusted to 0.5 McFarland turbidity. Amphotericin B served as the positive control, while the solvent and sterile distilled water served as negative controls. Plates were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 24 hours, and inhibition zones were measured in millimeters. Discover more Save on Rx Compare Lab Gear Study Chemistry Identify Plants Check Symptoms The results showed activity against four of the five tested species. The strongest effect appeared against Candida krusei, with a 35-millimeter inhibition zone compared with 20 millimeters for amphotericin B, a notable result because C. krusei is recognized for its intrinsic resistance to several conventional antifungal agents. Against Candida albicans, HIHPT produced a 28-millimeter zone while amphotericin B was recorded as resistant, meaning no measurable inhibition under the assay conditions. Candida lusitaniae showed a 22-millimeter zone with HIHPT, again with the reference drug recorded as resistant, and Candida tropicalis displayed a 16-millimeter zone for HIHPT versus 8 millimeters for amphotericin B. No activity was observed against Candida kefyr, and the DMSO negative control produced no inhibition for any strain, indicating the observed effects were attributable to the compound itself. Beyond planktonic growth, the team assessed biofilm formation using a crystal violet staining assay in 96-well polystyrene plates, measuring optical density at 620 nanometers after 24 hours of incubation. HIHPT inhibited biofilm formation across all five Candida isolates, with the highest inhibition against Candida albicans at 46.54 percent, followed by Candida kefyr at 36.46 percent, Candida lusitaniae at 33.87 percent, Candida krusei at 30.90 percent, and Candida tropicalis at 22.77 percent. Amphotericin B, by contrast, showed only weak biofilm inhibition against C. krusei and C. tropicalis and little or no inhibition against the remaining species under the same conditions. Because biofilm formation is a major virulence factor contributing to antifungal resistance and recurrent candidiasis, compounds that suppress it are considered promising leads, although the authors note that minimum inhibitory concentration, minimum fungicidal concentration, and mechanistic studies are still needed to validate the antifungal potential. Discover more Read Med Journals Find an OBGYN Study Biology On the computational side, the researchers docked HIHPT into the SARS-CoV-2 main protease, Mpro, using the Glide Standard Precision protocol in the Schrödinger Suite after validating the protocol by re-docking the co-crystallized ligand, methyl 4-sulfamoylbenzoate, with a root-mean-square deviation below 1.0 angstrom. HIHPT achieved a docking score of −5.913 kcal/mol and a binding energy of −45.525 kcal/mol, comparable to the reference ligand’s −6.518 kcal/mol and −47.112 kcal/mol. The docked pose formed two hydrogen bonds with Glu166 and Pro168, residues involved in substrate recognition and inhibitor stabilization, plus hydrophobic alkyl and pi-alkyl contacts with Met49 and Met165 in the S2 subsite. These docking results indicate a stable predicted binding conformation but do not by themselves demonstrate antiviral efficacy. Molecular dynamics simulations extended the docking analysis over 100 nanoseconds for two systems: the protease bound to the positive control compound Z18197050 and the protease bound to HIHPT. The root-mean-square deviation of C-alpha atoms settled near 2.4 angstroms for the control system and about 2.0 angstroms for the HIHPT complex, suggesting both systems equilibrated without major conformational change in the protease. Residues in contact with either ligand fluctuated by less than 6.0 angstroms. Because the simulation was implicit-solvent, water-mediated hydrogen-bonded interactions appeared with Glu166, Val186, Arg188, Gln189, Thr190, and Gln192 for the control, and with His41, Ser46, Asn142, Glu146, Gln189, and Thr190 for HIHPT, with Gln189 and Thr190 common to both complexes. Hydrophobic contacts involved Met49 and Met165 for the control and Met65 and Pro168 for the extracted compound. MM-GBSA binding free energy calculations on twenty snapshots taken at 5-nanosecond intervals showed consistently negative energies for both complexes. The control ranged from approximately −16.93 to −42.96 kcal/mol, with strain-corrected values from −17.37 to −44.01 kcal/mol, while HIHPT ranged from about −22.73 to −38.27 kcal/mol, or −23.73 to −39.01 kcal/mol with strain correction. The control generally bound more favorably, particularly near the end of the trajectory, but HIHPT maintained stable interaction energies throughout without significant fluctuations, and the small 1 to 3 kcal/mol differences between corrected and uncorrected values indicated minimal ligand conformational strain. The authors interpret this as thermodynamically favorable binding that warrants further biological validation rather than as evidence of inhibition. Additional quantum chemical and property calculations rounded out the profile. Density functional theory at the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) level yielded a HOMO-LUMO gap of 6.632 electron volts for HIHPT, close to the two reference ligands, with frontier orbitals localized on the cyclic portion of the molecule. Natural bond orbital charges identified the hydroxyl oxygen atoms as the most negative sites and hydroxyl hydrogens as the most positive, consistent with the molecular electrostatic potential map. Online property predictors estimated a cLogP near 5.3, no predicted mutagenicity, tumorigenicity, irritation, or reproductive toxicity risks, a drug-likeness score of −2.42, and a drug score of 0.21. A calculated intrinsic log P of 4.56 and intrinsic solubility of −4.85 log mol/L indicated a strongly lipophilic, poorly water-soluble neutral molecule that remains largely non-ionized between pH 1 and 12, which the authors note may limit aqueous dissolution and oral bioavailability absent formulation strategies. Taken together, the study positions HIHPT as a natural lead compound whose measured antifungal activity against clinical Candida isolates and predicted binding to SARS-CoV-2 Mpro justify further investigation. The authors themselves frame the conclusion cautiously: in vitro assays, docking, dynamics simulations, and property analyses revealed favorable biological activity, stable target interactions, and acceptable drug-like characteristics, but in vivo studies and clinical investigations are required to validate therapeutic efficacy and safety. For now, the findings add to the documented chemical diversity of Saharan medicinal flora and illustrate how traditional-use plants can yield structurally interesting triterpenoids for modern screening pipelines, while the gap between a laboratory inhibition zone and a clinically useful medicine remains substantial. supplementary_news.content: News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Insights Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event SUBSCRIBE Menu SUBSCRIBE Show Search News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Insights Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event Search Query Submit Search Press Releases SEKISUI Diagnostics Announces 510(k) Clearance and Launch of the OSOM® COVID-19/Flu A&B Combo Test October 28, 2026 | 2 min read Twitter LinkedIn Facebook Email Print SAN DIEGO, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SEKISUI Diagnostics, a global medical diagnostics manufacturer, has announced the launch of a 510(k) cleared rapid test to detect COVID-19 and Flu A&B in professional healthcare settings. The OSOM® COVID-19/Flu A&B Combo Test is a lateral flow immunochromatographic assay intended for the qualitative detection and differentiation of influenza A and influenza B nucleoprotein antigens and SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antigen directly in anterior nasal swab specimens from individuals with signs and symptoms of respiratory tract infection. CLIA-waived for point-of-care use, the OSOM COVID-19/Flu A&B Combo Test is manufactured in the USA and backed by an experienced technical services team of medical laboratory professionals. The OSOM COVID-19/Flu A&B Combo Test includes QC Inside®, a unique feature which maximizes the value of every kit by eliminating separate Quality Control (QC) costs and provides two additional patient tests for external QC at no charge. "With the Emergency Use Authorization ending, we know it is extremely important to continue to supply the market with the tools needed to diagnose respiratory infections quickly and accurately. We are pleased to be able to offer new customers and transition existing customers to a 510(k) cleared alternative as we enter the season, so they are well prepared before the termination takes effect." said Erica Blight, VP Strategy & Growth. As COVID-19 and influenza continue to present with overlapping symptoms, multiplex testing provides the advantage of identifying and differentiating multiple respiratory viruses from a single patient sample, helping support timely clinical decisions. SEKISUI Diagnostics is a well-known provider of many rapid diagnostic solutions to the professional and home testing markets through a portfolio of tests under the OSOM and Metrix® brands. About SEKISUI Diagnostics: With over 40 years of experience, SEKISUI Diagnostics' mission is to provide intelligent solutions to enhance life with science and improve the health of all people. We supply innovative medical diagnostics globally to physicians, hospitals, laboratories and alternate testing locations. Our product lines include clinical chemistry reagents, point-of-care tests, pre-analytic systems, contract design and manufacturing as well as enzymes and specialty biochemicals. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Immune Complexes of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and Nucleocapsid Drive Inflammation by October 29, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Immune Complexes of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and Nucleocapsid Drive Inflammation Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Immune complexes built from SARS-CoV-2 RNA, the viral nucleocapsid protein and anti-nucleocapsid IgG1 antibodies can drive the runaway inflammation seen in severe COVID-19, according to a laboratory study published in PLOS Pathogens. Researchers found that when these RNA-containing complexes are taken up by primary human monocytes, the cells produce inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in a response that depends on Fcγ receptors and is partially dependent on toll-like receptor 8. The team, led by Johannes S. Gach and colleagues, traced how this phagocytic uptake translates into tissue damage. When monocytes were stimulated with the RNA-containing immune complexes, the inflammatory response they mounted caused endothelial dysfunction in vascularized micro-organs, laboratory models of human blood vessels. This links antibody-assisted clearance of viral material to a hallmark of severe disease: injury to the vascular lining. The study also addressed where such complexes come from. Using nasopharyngeal samples from SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals, the researchers captured SARS-CoV-2 RNA and nucleocapsid protein with an anti-nucleocapsid monoclonal antibody without using lysing reagents. That result indicates the RNA and nucleocapsid complexes exist outside of virions and cells in the airways, making them available to form inflammatory immune complexes with circulating antibodies. Discover more Study Biology Find Treatments Get Health Tips Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Consistent with a role for IgG-mediated inflammatory clearance in disease severity, the authors report that during an early wave of COVID-19, higher anti-nucleocapsid IgG:IgM ratios were associated with more severe clinical outcomes. They suggest this pattern fits a model in which inflammatory, IgG-driven phagocytic clearance of nucleic acid-containing immune complexes contributes to pathogenesis, while non-inflammatory, IgM-mediated clearance might mitigate it. As an observational association from one early pandemic wave, this finding supports but does not prove that mechanism. The authors conclude that RNA-containing immune complexes may play a role in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19. Because all pathogenic viruses encode nucleic acid-binding proteins similar to nucleocapsid, and these proteins often elicit antibody responses, they propose that inflammatory clearance of nucleic acid-containing immune complexes could also contribute to severity in other viral infections. As the work relies on in vitro monocyte assays, micro-organ models and patient sample analyses rather than direct clinical intervention studies, the findings define a plausible inflammatory mechanism and generate hypotheses for future research into severe viral disease rather than establishing treatment effects. Subject of Research: How SARS-CoV-2 RNA-containing immune complexes drive inflammatory cytokine production and endothelial dysfunction in severe COVID-19. Why is the DOJ collaborating with the IRS on fraud investigations? topics: COVID-19 Fraud Department of Justice Oregon Demand letters Recovery Internal Revenue Service Fraud.gov PORTLAND, Ore. (KATU) — Federal prosecutors in Oregon have recovered nearly $16 million as part of an ongoing crackdown on COVID-19 relief fraud, and officials say that number could grow significantly by the end of the year. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, federal officials are preparing to send thousands of demand letters to people whose COVID-19 relief loans showed potential signs of fraud. “Over the next few days, over 2,300 demand letters totaling nearly $97 million are being sent to applicants whose loans included indicators of fraud,” Inspector General William Kirk said. The letters seek repayment of funds associated with potentially fraudulent loans, although the $97 million has not yet been recovered. RELATED: Trump administration uncovers $1.2B in suspected fraud tied to COVID-era contracts Powered By 10 Sec Feds in Oregon confirm nearly $16M recovered in ongoing COVID-19 relief fraud crackdown Next Stay Federal prosecutors say their efforts to identify and hold accountable people suspected of fraudulently obtaining federal relief funds are far from over. U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford said investigators have continued uncovering new cases in recent weeks. “Because it's still happening. That's 10 more cases, $34 million in losses and $7.2 million in recovery in just the last 45 days,” Bradford said. The DOJ is also working directly with the Internal Revenue Service to identify additional suspected fraud cases across Oregon. Officials say they have already received thousands of tips related to suspected fraud in the state, helping investigators identify potential cases. Kirk emphasized that the investigations are about recovering taxpayer money and preventing future fraud. “It's your money. These are taxpayer dollars that have been stolen from you, the taxpayer. And anything that we can recover and anything that we can deter going forward, any behavior like that going forward is gonna be to your benefit,” Kirk said. Federal officials say they will continue pursuing suspected fraud and recovering federal relief funds as investigations move forward. supplementary_news.content: 24/7 LiveChicago & Suburban Cook Co.North SuburbsWest SuburbsSouth SuburbsNW Indiana 60° COVID 19 Chicago unveils COVID-19 memorial monument and park in Illinois Medical District It's located near Polk Street, Ogden Avenue and Damen Avenue in the Illinois Medical District. ByEvelyn Holmes Tuesday, October 27, 2026 5:16PM Share Follow ABC7 on Google CHICAGO (WLS) -- City leaders, health care workers and community members gathered on the West Side for the official unveiling of the COVID-19 Memorial Monument. ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch The monument and park were designed as a place for reflection and healing. It's located near the intersection of Polk Street, Ogden Avenue and Damen Avenue. The site, once a vacant space, was transformed into a tribute in the center of the Illinois Medical District, which was established in 1941. The project was made possible through $4.95 million in funding and grant support. "This is your park, come often, find a moment of peace and make it your own," said Allyson Hansen, chief executive officer and executive director of the Illinois Medical District Commission. Top Stories All 9 people died on jet that crashed into Florida neighborhood, transportation secretary says 28 minutes ago Woman shot to death in Oak Park, police say Other women contacted police about previous incidents with Packers' Josh Jacobs after his arrest 3 hours ago For many attendees, the ceremony served as recognition of a period marked by grief and hardship. The monument, designed to symbolize community resilience, is the result of more than a year of work by the COVID-19 Monument Commission. A Chicago-based volunteer-led initiative dedicated to honoring those who died during the pandemic while recognizing the contributions of essential workers. Following an international competition, the commission selected a design featuring illuminated stainless steel dandelion sculptures intended to symbolize remembrance, hope and renewal. It’s located near Polk Street, Ogden Avenue and Damen Avenue in the Illinois Medical District. Organizers said they hope the memorial monument and park will serve as a sacred space for generations to come, helping ensure that the lessons of the pandemic and the lost lives are not forgotten. supplementary_news.content: Understanding the latest COVID strain AS we move into the colder months, COVID-19 is once again attracting attention with reports of a variant being referred to in the media as 'American COVID'. For many people the pandemic may feel like a distant memory but coronavirus continues to circulate, evolve and occasionally cause serious illness. So what is this new strain, how does it affect us and what can we do to protect ourselves and our families? The variant attracting attention is known as XFG, also called Stratus. It belongs to the Omicron family of coronavirus variants and was first identified in January 2025. It has subsequently spread internationally and been detected in the UK. The term 'American COVID' is somewhat misleading. It does not mean that the virus originated in America or that it is confined to the United States. The nickname reflects its association with the country where it was first identified in media coverage. XFG has genetic changes that may help it evade some immunity acquired through previous infection or vaccination. This may contribute to its ability to spread. However, there is currently no convincing evidence that XFG causes more severe illness than other circulating variants. The UK Health Security Agency continues to monitor its behaviour and the wider impact of COVID-19. COVID-19 spreads predominantly through the air. Infected individuals release respiratory particles when breathing, speaking, coughing or sneezing. Transmission is particularly likely in crowded, poorly ventilated indoor environments. People can spread the virus before developing symptoms and some infections remain asymptomatic. The clinical presentation of the current variants is generally similar to that of previous Omicron strains. Common symptoms include a sore throat, fever, chills, cough, runny nose, nasal congestion, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, nausea, diarrhoea or changes in taste and smell. Symptoms may initially resemble a common cold or influenza. Most people experience a mild illness and recover without needing hospital treatment. Nevertheless, older people, pregnant women, individuals with weakened immune systems and those with underlying conditions such as heart disease, diabetes or chronic lung disease remain particularly vulnerable to complications. For most otherwise healthy people, treatment involves rest, adequate fluids and appropriate medicines to relieve symptoms, such as paracetamol when needed. However, people at increased risk of severe illness should seek medical advice promptly if they develop symptoms. Antiviral treatments, including Paxlovid, may be appropriate for eligible patients, particularly when started early. These medicines require clinical assessment because they can interact with other medications. Severe COVID-19 can cause pneumonia, respiratory failure, blood clots and damage to organs. Although uncommon, these complications can be life-threatening. Another important consequence is long COVID in which symptoms persist for weeks or months after the initial infection. These may include exhaustion, breathlessness, muscle pain and difficulty concentrating, sometimes significantly affecting a person's ability to work or undertake everyday activities. Vaccination remains one of our most effective measures against severe COVID-19, hospitalisation and death. Although vaccines may not completely prevent infection, they help reduce the risk of serious illness. Eligible individuals, particularly older adults and people with underlying medical conditions, should follow current NHS vaccination advice. Simple measures also make a difference. Staying at home when unwell, improving ventilation, washing hands regularly and wearing a well-fitting mask in crowded indoor spaces when appropriate can reduce transmission. If symptoms develop, consider testing, particularly if you are vulnerable or live with someone at increased risk. The emergence of another coronavirus variant should remind us that COVID-19 has not disappeared. However, the available evidence does not suggest that the American COVID variant represents a return to the early days of the pandemic. We now have vaccines, treatments, improved clinical understanding and experience of managing respiratory infections. For Worcester and the surrounding communities, the message is straightforward — remain informed, take sensible precautions, protect those most vulnerable and seek medical advice when necessary. COVID-19 is now part of our continuing public health landscape. With awareness and proportionate action, we can reduce its impact while continuing to live our lives. Our columnist Dr Jason Seewoodhary is a former Worcestershire GP
